Phoenicia is the stretch of the eastern Mediterranean coast around Tyre and Sidon; Cyprus is a large island in the sea; Antioch is farther north, the capital of the province of Syria and the third-largest city of the Roman Empire, with a population of about half a million—Greeks, Syrians, and Jews living together, a thoroughly Gentile city.

The seeds of a dandelion are scattered by the wind; the stronger the wind, the farther the seeds fly. Stephen’s martyrdom and Saul’s persecution were that wind, scattering the disciples; they thought it was disaster, but God used it to sow seed three hundred miles away in Antioch. “Affliction” and “traveled as far as” are in the same sentence—affliction is not the end of the story but the reason the story traveled far.
Yet this group “spoke the word to no one except to Jews only.” They had the gospel and were willing to go, but their audience stayed within their own people.
• The wind blows the seed far: affliction is not the end but God’s way of sending you farther.
• Going far, speaking narrow: being willing to go out does not mean being willing to speak to different people.
II. “Some of them… men of Cyprus and Cyrene… spoke to the Greeks, preaching the Lord Jesus”—Nameless People Opened the Greatest Door

Verses 20–21: “But there were some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, who, when they had come to Antioch, spoke to the Greeks also, preaching the Lord Jesus. The hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number believed and turned to the Lord.”

Luke did not record their names. They were Jews from Cyprus and Cyrene (North Africa), people already scattered abroad who dealt with Gentiles every day, their frame a little smaller than that of the Jews in Jerusalem. Arriving in Antioch, they spoke “to the Greeks also.”

Notice they preached “the Lord Jesus,” not “the Christ.” To Jews one had to prove that Jesus was the Messiah; Greeks did not understand “Messiah,” so they preached “the Lord Jesus”—He is Lord. The gospel did not change; the way of telling it came close to the hearers.

Then, “The hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number believed and turned to the Lord.” A group with no names and no apostolic standing opened a door greater than Cornelius’s house, because the hand of the Lord was with them. God’s system is not built by people with names but by a group of people emptied of self—they need not be recorded; they need only the Lord’s presence.
• Nameless people: the greatest door in Acts was opened by nameless people.
• The hand of the Lord was with them: not who spoke, but who was with the speakers.
III. “When he came and saw the grace of God, was glad”—Eyes That See Grace

Verses 22–24: the news reached Jerusalem, and the church “sent out Barnabas.” The choice was wise—Barnabas himself was a Cypriot (Acts 4:36), a countryman of those who preached in Antioch. When he arrived, “he saw the grace of God, and was glad.”

A man coming from Jerusalem to a Gentile metropolis where all kinds of people lived could have seen many problems: not circumcised, not keeping dietary rules, meeting the wrong way. What Barnabas saw was “the grace of God”—and then he was glad. His eyes first saw what God had done, not what people had done wrong.

So he “exhorted them all, that with purpose of heart they should remain near to the Lord.” “Exhorted” is exactly the meaning of his name—son of encouragement. He did not go to correct but to strengthen. Luke gives him three assessments: a good man, full of the Holy Spirit, and of faith. A person filled with the Holy Spirit, looking at people, sees grace.
• See grace first: arriving at a new place, first see what God has done, not what people have done wrong.
• Go to strengthen, not to correct: exhorting everyone to remain near the Lord was Barnabas’s first work.
IV. “He went out to Tarsus to look for Saul”—Finding the Man and Giving Up the Place
Verses 25 and the first half of 26: “Barnabas went out to Tarsus to look for Saul. When he had found him, he brought him to Antioch.”

From the time Saul was sent back to Tarsus by the brothers (Acts 9:30), about ten years had passed, and Acts had said not one word of him. Barnabas remembered him. “Look for” in the original is “search diligently”—Tarsus is not small, and Saul may not have been easy to find, but Barnabas went and found him.

Because he saw that the work in Antioch was too great for one man, and also saw that Saul was a vessel God had prepared for the Gentiles (Acts 9:27). He did not think, “This is my field,” but only, “Who is best suited here?” He went and found a man more gifted than himself, and from then on Luke’s way of writing slowly changed from “Barnabas and Saul” to “Paul and Barnabas.”

This is giving up self—for Jesus, for others, not for oneself. In chapter 4 Barnabas sold a field; now he gave up a place. A man who could let go of property could later let go of position. Self-denial is not having nothing but entering the limitless: Barnabas gave up one Antioch, but through Paul gained the whole Gentile world.

“For a whole year they were gathered together with the assembly, and taught many people.” After a revival, without teaching, however many people there are, they cannot stand firm. The foundation of the Antioch church was a solid year of feeding on the word.
• Remember the forgotten: Saul, whom no one had mentioned for ten years—Barnabas went and found him.
• Give up the place: not asking “Is this my field?” but only “Who is best suited here?”
V. “The disciples were first called Christians at Antioch”—A New Name
The second half of verse 26: “The disciples were first called Christians in Antioch.”

“Christians” in the original is “those belonging to Christ,” a name given by outsiders and probably carrying mockery at first. In Jerusalem the disciples were seen as a sect within Judaism; in Antioch, Jews and Greeks mixed together and outsiders could no longer call them “Jews,” so they had to find a new name. And the most obvious mark on them was Christ.

This is the best praise. When outsiders looked at this group, they could not see Jew or Greek, only Christ. A name is seen: the apostles looked at Joseph and saw “son of encouragement”; outsiders in Antioch looked at these disciples and saw “those belonging to Christ.” It is no longer I but Christ—when a group’s “self” has receded out of sight, what people see is only Christ.
• A name outsiders gave: they could not see Jew or Greek, only Christ.
• A name is seen: what is the most obvious mark on you?
The Light of the 321 Principles: God’s System Is Built by Nameless People and People Who Give Up Their Place
Antioch is the turning point of Acts; all three of Paul’s missionary journeys set out from here. But how was this church built?

Not by apostles but by a group of nameless people scattered by affliction; not by planned mission but by the Lord being with them. Then Barnabas came, who saw grace rather than problems, strengthened rather than corrected, found a man more gifted than himself, and then stepped back to second place. In this church no one was grasping for position, so what outsiders saw was only Christ.

Building God’s system is not about organizational structure but about the domain formed by a group of people who let Jesus be King. There are two kinds of such people: the nameless, willing to go far and speak to those unlike themselves, with no need to be remembered; and the named, like Barnabas, willing to give their names to others. What the two share is self-denial. People living for self build their own system, with their own name at the center; people emptied of self build God’s system, with the name of Christ at the center—so the name people gave them was Christians.
a: Let the Wind Blow You Far
Affliction is not the end; ask where God wants to send you.
Speak to Different People
After being willing to go out, be willing also to speak to those unlike you.
See Grace First
In a new environment, first see what God has done, then everything else.
Go Find the Forgotten
Think of a Saul no one has mentioned in ten years, and go find him.
Let People See Only Christ
May the most obvious mark on you be His name.
q: When Barnabas arrived at Antioch, he “saw the grace of God, and was glad.” Recall a new environment or group you recently entered: did you first see grace, or problems?
Is there a “Saul in Tarsus” around you—someone gifted but forgotten for a long time? If going to find him would mean giving up some of your place, are you willing?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that the wind of one affliction blew the seed to Antioch; thank You for using a group of nameless people to open the door through which the gospel went out to the world; thank You for giving Barnabas, with eyes that saw grace and a heart willing to give up his place.
Lord Jesus, we confess that we are willing to go out yet often speak only to our own people; when we arrive at a new place we often see problems first and seldom first see Your grace; and we often cling to our own field and our own name, unable to remember the Saul no one has mentioned in ten years. Forgive us. Give us the heart of the nameless, with no need to be remembered, only needing Your presence; and give us the heart of Barnabas, willing to go find someone more suited than ourselves and willing to step back to second place. May our “self” recede out of sight, so that when people look at us they see only You—may we be worthy of the name “those belonging to Christ.” In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Now in these days, prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch.
One of them named Agabus stood up, and indicated by the Spirit that there should be a great famine all over the world, which also happened in the days of Claudius.
As any of the disciples had plenty, each determined to send relief to the brothers who lived in Judea;
which they also did, sending it to the elders by the hands of Barnabas and Saul.
b: In the last devotion, the disciples in Antioch received a new name—Christians, those belonging to Christ. When outsiders looked at them, they could not see Jew or Greek, only Christ.

In this devotion Luke uses four verses to tell us how a group called Christians lived their days. No miracles, no visions—only a piece of news, a decision, a journey. Yet within these four verses is the first outstretched hand of a newborn church, reaching toward the Jerusalem that had first brought them the gospel.
I. “Prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch”—Between Two Cities, There Is a Road
Verse 27: “In these days, prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch.”

Jerusalem is in the highlands and Antioch on the plain to the north, so it says “came down.” New Testament prophets were not fortune-tellers but people moved by the Holy Spirit to speak God’s word, to exhort and comfort the church (1 Corinthians 14:3). They came from Jerusalem not to inspect or to govern but to serve.

Note the traffic between the two cities. In verse 22 Jerusalem sent Barnabas down, in verse 27 prophets came down, and in verse 30 Antioch sent men up. Between the mother church and the new church there was not top-down control but the going to and fro of brothers. Antioch did not set itself up as a separate kingdom, and Jerusalem did not hold on tightly. God’s system is not one city ruling another but a road between two cities that people often travel.
• The prophets came to serve: those who came from Jerusalem came not to govern but to give.
• A road between the two places: not top-down control but brothers going back and forth.
II. “Signified by the Spirit that there should be a great famine all over the world”—A Prophecy Is for Preparing
Verse 28: “One of them named Agabus stood up and indicated by the Spirit that there should be a great famine all over the world. This happened in the days of Claudius.”

Agabus will appear again in chapter 21, binding himself with Paul’s belt and prophesying that Paul would be bound (Acts 21:10–11). He was a true prophet whose words came to pass. Claudius was the Roman emperor, reigning from AD 41 to 54; the historian Josephus records that around AD 46 a severe famine did occur in Judea. When Luke writes “this happened,” he is telling the reader: check it, it is true.

But notice the purpose of the Spirit’s foretelling. The Spirit did not say, “A famine is coming, hurry and stockpile grain,” nor “This is God’s judgment.” He only indicated. Then the disciples in Antioch understood for themselves: when famine struck the world, the ones who would suffer most would be the brothers in Judea—the Jerusalem church was already poor, under persecution, with many widows to support. A prophecy is not for causing panic but for preparing; not for looking after oneself first but for thinking of others first.

The Holy Spirit as my guide here does not look like “the Spirit told me something startling” but “the Spirit told me something, and so I know what to do for whom.” The result of guidance is always action, and action for others.
• Stands up to checking: it happened in the days of Claudius; what the Bible records is real.
• A prophecy is for preparing: on hearing it, the first thought is not what shall I do but who will suffer most.
III. “Every one of the disciples determined to send relief, according to his ability, to the brothers who lived in Judea”—A New Church’s First Action Was to Give
Verse 29: “As any of the disciples had plenty, each determined to send relief to the brothers who lived in Judea.”

“Determined”—no one asked them; they decided for themselves. “According to his ability”—not a fixed amount but whatever they had; those with more gave more, those with less gave less, and everyone had a share. “To the brothers who lived in Judea”—this group, mostly Gentile disciples, called the Jews “brothers.”

Think about the direction of this. The gospel went from Jerusalem to Antioch; now money went from Antioch back to Jerusalem. Spiritual grace flowed outward; material supply flowed back. Paul later put this principle clearly: “For if the Gentiles have been made partakers of their spiritual things, they owe it to them to serve them also in fleshly things” (Romans 15:27). Antioch had not yet read Romans, and they were already doing it.

A human body is one. When a hand is hurt, blood naturally flows to it; no one holds a meeting to decide whether to send blood. The disciples in Antioch were like this: when they heard the brothers in Judea were going to suffer, blood flowed there. This is the best mark of a new church—not how many people or gifts it has, but that its first outward act was to give, and to give to those unlike themselves. People matter more than tasks, and relationships more than things: what they gave away in money bought them a family that from then on no longer divided Jew and Gentile.
• Determined, not asked: no one spoke up; they decided themselves.
• Blood flows to the wound: in a healthy body, supply is natural and needs no meeting to decide.
IV. “Sending it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Saul”—Trustworthy People, Trustworthy Route
Verse 30: “This they also did, sending it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Saul.”

“This they also did”—having determined, they did it. They chose two men to send: Barnabas and Saul. Two traveling together was the early church’s consistent way of handling money—transparent, checkable, mutually witnessed. Paul later insisted: “taking thought for things honorable, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men” (2 Corinthians 8:21). In matters of money, the more spiritual a person is, the more openly he must walk.

Sent “to the elders”—this is the first time the word “elders” is used of the church. The apostles may have been scattered by persecution, and the Jerusalem church was managed by elders. Antioch handed the money to them without specifying use and without sending anyone to supervise; once handed over, it was handed over.

Look again at Barnabas. In chapter 4 he laid the money from selling his field at the apostles’ feet; now he carried Antioch’s offering to the elders. All his life he did the same thing: hand things over and keep nothing. And this time Saul was at his side—the man he had found at Tarsus. This was Saul’s first errand for the church, and it was carrying money to brothers in need. The man who would go on three missionary journeys and write half the New Testament had as his first assignment delivering relief. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: God’s order of training a person is always this.
• Two to carry it: walking openly in money matters is the duty of spiritual people.
• The first assignment was delivering relief: God trains great vessels beginning with faithfulness in small things.
The Light of the 321 Principles: God’s System Is Where Grace Flows

Chapter 11 began with an argument—the brothers in Jerusalem questioning Peter for eating with Gentiles; chapter 11 ends with a journey carrying money—Gentile disciples sending an offering to supply the Jewish brothers. From “How could you eat with them?” to “We are sending them grain,” there was only one chapter in between. God works much faster than people’s frames come down.

Building God’s system is not about organizational structure but about the domain formed by a group of people who let Jesus be King. This domain has one obvious mark: grace flows within it—the spiritual flowing outward, the material flowing back, with no end blocked. Wherever it is blocked, there is surely a “self” there: my church, my resources, people like us. The disciples in Antioch were not blocked, because within them there was no “we Gentiles” and “they Jews”—they called each other brothers.

What self-denial looks like here is not said but sent: according to each one’s ability, putting money in the hands of two trustworthy men, to be delivered to elders they had never met, to supply brothers they had never met. For Jesus, for others, not for oneself. Such a group is worthy of that name—Christians.
a: Keep a Road Between Two Places
Don’t set yourself up as a separate kingdom, and don’t hold on tightly; keep going back and forth.
On Hearing a Prophecy, Think of Others
When the Spirit indicates something, the first thought is who will suffer most.
Determine, and Do It
Don’t wait to be asked; decide yourself, and once decided, do it.
Let Blood Flow to the Wound
Where there is need in the body, supply naturally goes there.
Walk Openly in Money Matters
Handle it with two together, and once handed over, don’t grasp it.
q: The last time you heard that some place or group was in difficulty, was your first thought “Will I be affected?” or “Who will suffer most, and what can I supply?”

Antioch sent its offering back to the Jerusalem that had first preached the gospel to them. Is there a person or group who once supplied you spiritually and now has material or practical need, to whom you could “determine, and do it”?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for opening a road between Jerusalem and Antioch that people often travel; thank You for indicating the famine beforehand by the Spirit, not to cause panic but to prepare, and to make people think of others first. Thank You for letting a group of disciples who had just received a new name make their first outward act giving.
Lord Jesus, we confess that we often set ourselves up as a separate kingdom, blocking the gospel and our resources inside “people like us”; when we hear of difficulty, our first thought is often what shall I do, seldom who will suffer most. Forgive us. Make us a healthy body, where blood flows to wherever there is a wound, with no need of a meeting to decide; make us, like the disciples at Antioch, determine, according to each one’s ability, and then do it. And make us open in money matters, no longer grasping what we have handed over. May our self-denial be not only spoken but sent; be King among us, so that grace flows within us, blocked by no “self.” In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Now about that time, King Herod stretched out his hands to oppress some of the assembly.
He killed James, the brother of John, with the sword.
When he saw that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to seize Peter also. This was during the days of unleavened bread.
When he had arrested him, he put him in prison, and delivered him to four squads of four soldiers each to guard him, intending to bring him out to the people after the Passover.
Peter therefore was kept in the prison, but constant prayer was made by the assembly to God for him.
b: In the last devotion, the prophet Agabus stood up in Antioch and signified by the Spirit that a great famine would come over all the world. The disciples in Antioch did not look after themselves first; instead, each according to his ability gave money, and sent it by Barnabas and Saul to Jerusalem to relieve the brothers in Judea. It was a warm picture: the Gentile church and the Jewish church becoming one family over sack after sack of grain.

But Luke’s camera turns, and chapter 12 opens with a sword. The famine had not passed, and persecution came first. What Antioch sent was grain, yet Jerusalem was bleeding. The gospel is not a story of smooth sailing; the church has always advanced between the edge of the sword and grace.
I. “About that time, Herod the king stretched out his hands to oppress some of the assembly”—A King Who Knew How to Please People

This Herod was not the Herod the Great who killed the babies of Bethlehem, nor Herod Antipas who killed John the Baptist, but Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great. He grew up in Rome from childhood, educated with the sons of the imperial house, and was an old acquaintance of Caligula and Claudius, who later became emperors. In AD 41 Claudius added Judea and Samaria to his realm, giving him a territory nearly as large as his grandfather’s.

Agrippa understood one thing well: to sit securely among the Jews, he had to make the Jews like him. He kept the law strictly, often went up to the temple to offer sacrifices, and played the devout Jewish king everywhere. “Stretched out his hands” in the original is “laid hands on to harm”; this hand was stretched out not because the church had committed any crime but because striking this group could win applause.
• The politics of pleasing people: the standard by which he decided was not right and wrong but “the Jews like this.”
• People of self watch the wind: a person centered on his own seat trades other people’s lives for his own applause.
II. “He killed James the brother of John with the sword”—The First of the Twelve to Be Martyred

Verse 2 is a single sentence, yet it is a heavy page in church history: James was dead, the first of the twelve apostles to be martyred for the Lord. “Killed with the sword” means beheading, a Roman form of execution, not the Jewish stoning.

This James was the son of Zebedee, with John one of the “sons of thunder,” who had been with Peter and John on the Mount of Transfiguration and in Gethsemane. His mother once asked the Lord to let her two sons sit at His right and left, and the Lord asked them, “Are you able to drink the cup that I drink?” They said they were able. The Lord said, “You shall indeed drink the cup that I drink” (Mark 10:38–39). Some years later, that cup was indeed placed in James’s hands.

Luke uses only one verse, without embellishment or explanation. In the same chapter Peter was wonderfully delivered while James was killed; the same God, two men equally loved by the church, with completely different endings. The Bible does not defend God, nor does it beautify this. This reminds us: believing in the Lord is not buying insurance. What the Lord promised is to be with us, not that nothing will ever happen to us.
• Face it honestly: the Lord did not promise that everyone would get out of prison; He promised that everyone is in His hand.
• The cup is handed by the Lord: the cup James drank was one the Lord Himself had asked him about; no difficulty in our hands passes without the Lord’s hand.
III. “Those were the days of unleavened bread”—Peter Seized at Passover

Seeing that killing James pleased the people, Herod went on to seize Peter. Luke notes specially that it was the days of unleavened bread, the seven-day Passover festival. Herod respected the festival rule and did not execute during the festival, intending to bring Peter out “to the people” after the festival—making the execution a public performance.

The timing is meaningful. A few years earlier, in the same city and at the same festival, the Lord Jesus was seized, tried, and crucified. Now Peter was put in prison during the same Passover. Disciples in the world will not walk a smoother road than the Lord’s.

Look also at Herod’s arrangements: four squads of soldiers, four to a squad, sixteen men in all, changing shifts day and night. A fisherman, guarded by a small unit. Worldly power is always like this—seemingly watertight, yet in fact exposing its fear.
• The road the Lord walked: the festival at which the disciple was seized was the festival of the Lord’s suffering; to follow the Lord is to walk in His footsteps.
• See through power’s bluster: sixteen soldiers guarding one man shows that the one afraid is not Peter but Herod.
IV. “But constant prayer was being made by the assembly to God for him”—The Word “But,” an Unseen Battle
Verse 5 has a turn: “Peter therefore was kept in the prison, but constant prayer was being made by the assembly to God for him.”

On one side were the prison, the chains, sixteen soldiers, and a king holding the power of life and death; on the other, a group of ordinary people with no weapons, no backing, no lawyer. What could they do? Luke says they did one thing: pray. “Constant” in the original has the sense of “stretched to the limit”; Luke’s Gospel records the Lord in Gethsemane praying “more earnestly” (Luke 22:44), using the same root. This was not routine intercession but the whole church stretching itself to the extreme, holding on to God and not letting go.

Imagine the family waiting outside an intensive care unit. They cannot lend a hand to anything going on inside; all they can do is wait outside and pray outside. But such waiting is never “being able to do nothing”; it is placing the heaviest matter into the hand that can truly act. The church’s situation was exactly this: they could not open the prison gate, but they knew the God who could.

When James was killed, the church may also have prayed, and the result was martyrdom. So what use is prayer? It is of use—because the purpose of prayer has never been to control the outcome but to hand the outcome back to God.
• The faith of “but”: the more watertight the circumstances, the more the church should turn to God rather than to its own calculations.
• Prayer is not a remote control: we do not use prayer to manipulate God; we use prayer to acknowledge that He is God.
The Light of the 321 Principles: The Focus Is on God, Not on Herod

These five verses set before us the most real situation: a king who pleased people, a real sword, an apostle really dead, a real prison. The church neither denied these nor was swallowed by them, because their focus was not on circumstances but on God.

A life lived for self, meeting Herod, reacts first with the head: how to smooth over connections, how to avoid the wind, how to protect oneself. Relying on my own head, the more I think the more anxious I become, because counting it up, a person really holds few cards. A life emptied of self, meeting Herod, reacts first with the heart relying on the Holy Spirit: first return to God, and pray earnestly. Using the heart makes the heart glad, not because the prison gate has already opened, but because the King in the heart has not changed—however great Herod is, he is not the king in my heart.

James was martyred and Peter imprisoned, and the church did not therefore question “Is God still in control?”; instead, it prayed more earnestly. This is the reaction only of a group who let Jesus be King: first God, then myself, then people, then tasks. They did not first deal with the “task” of Herod, but first returned before God. God’s system is established, again and again, in prayers like these.
a: See Through the Wind
Herod decided by whether the Jews liked it; do I have a decision today made to please people rather than to please God?
Face It Honestly
The Lord did not promise everyone would leave prison; James drank the cup the Lord drank; I am willing to accept the cup the Lord measures out to me.
Recognize the Footsteps
Peter was seized in the festival of the Lord’s suffering; if the hard road I walk is the road of following the Lord, then I have not gone wrong.
Turn to God First
Before a watertight situation, my first act is not calculation but prayer.
Constantly
Not asking for peace with the lips, but the whole person stretched to the limit, truly placing the matter in God’s hand.
q: James was martyred and Peter was delivered; the same God gave two different endings. Can you accept that God’s work in you may not come in the way you expect? Which kind of ending are you least willing to accept?
Facing a “watertight” difficulty, recall your most recent reaction: calculate first, or pray first? How does “constant prayer” differ from your usual praying?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for letting us see that the church did not grow up in a greenhouse. No sooner had Antioch’s grain arrived than Herod’s sword fell; James was martyred and Peter was imprisoned, yet Your church did not scatter but prayed to You earnestly. Give us also such a church and such faith.
Lord, we confess that when trouble comes we often use our heads first and rely on ourselves first, thinking first how to smooth things over and protect ourselves, leaving You last. Forgive us. Teach us, like the church of that time, to move our focus away from Herod and fix our eyes on You; teach us not to use prayer to manipulate You but to use prayer to acknowledge that You are King. Whether the road You take in us is James’s road or Peter’s road, we ask that You be glorified in us. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: The same night when Herod was about to bring him out, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains. Guards in front of the door kept the prison.
And behold, an angel of the Lord stood by him, and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side, and woke him up, saying, “Stand up quickly!” His chains fell off his hands.
The angel said to him, “Get dressed and put on your sandals.” He did so. He said to him, “Put on your cloak and follow me.”
And he went out and followed him. He didn’t know that what was being done by the angel was real, but thought he saw a vision.

When they were past the first and the second guard, they came to the iron gate that leads into the city, which opened to them by itself. They went out, and went down one street, and immediately the angel departed from him.
When Peter had come to himself, he said, “Now I truly know that the Lord has sent out his angel and delivered me out of the hand of Herod, and from everything the Jewish people were expecting.”
Thinking about that, he came to the house of Mary, the mother of John who was called Mark, where many were gathered together and were praying.
When Peter knocked at the door of the gate, a servant girl named Rhoda came to answer.
When she recognized Peter’s voice, she didn’t open the gate for joy, but ran in, and reported that Peter was standing in front of the gate.
They said to her, “You are crazy!” But she insisted that it was so. They said, “It is his angel.”
But Peter continued knocking. When they had opened, they saw him, and were amazed.

But he, beckoning to them with his hand to be silent, declared to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. He said, “Tell these things to James and to the brothers.” Then he departed and went to another place.
b: The last devotion stopped on one word, “but”: Peter was kept in prison, but the church prayed earnestly to God for him. On one side, chains and sixteen soldiers; on the other, a group of kneeling people.

Today Luke tells us what happened that night. The whole narrative has two scenes: the first in the prison, where the Lord’s angel comes in; the second at Mary’s house, where Peter stands outside knocking. Interestingly, the prison’s iron gate opened by itself, while the wooden door of the church was slow to be opened by anyone. God’s work often goes farther and faster than our prayers.
I. “The same night… sleeping between two soldiers”—The Man to Die Tomorrow Was Asleep Tonight

Herod was going to bring him out tomorrow; he was bound with two chains, each chained to a soldier on either side, with guards at the door. In such a situation, what did Peter do? He slept. And he slept so soundly that the angel had to strike him on the side to wake him.

How could he sleep? Perhaps he remembered what the risen Lord had said to him by the sea: “when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you, and carry you where you don’t want to go” (John 21:18). The Lord had said “when you are old,” and he was not old yet. The Lord’s word became his pillow. The psalm says, “He gives sleep to his loved ones” (Psalm 127:2).

Sleep is a very honest gauge. If the mouth says I have entrusted it but at night one tosses and turns, that shows the matter is still in one’s own hand. Peter’s sleep was the sleep of self-denial—what happens tomorrow was not his business but the Lord’s.
• The evidence of entrusting: not on the lips but on the pillow; only one who can sleep has truly let go.
• The Lord’s word as pillow: keep what the Lord has said in your heart; when trouble comes, that word will keep watch for you at night.
II. “Rise up quickly”—What God Can Do, God Does; What People Can Do, People Do

The angel gave a series of commands: get up, put on your belt, put on your sandals, wrap your cloak around you, follow me. The chains falling off was God’s act; belting, putting on sandals, and putting on the cloak were Peter’s actions. God did not carry the sleeping Peter out bodily; He wanted him to stand up himself, put on his sandals himself, and walk himself.

Notice the time: it was Passover night. Moses’ instruction to Israel for eating the Passover lamb was: “with your belt on your waist, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and you shall eat it in haste” (Exodus 12:11). Now, on a night of the same festival, the angel said to Peter: put on your belt, put on your sandals. This was Peter’s personal exodus. When God struck Egypt, Israel still had to walk out themselves; tonight God broke the chains, and Peter still had to take the steps himself.
• Grace does not cancel responsibility: He breaks the chains; you put on your own sandals.
• Obedience between waking and sleeping: Peter “didn’t know that what was done by the angel was real,” yet he did as told. Obey first; understanding often comes afterward.
III. “The gate opened to them by itself”—Guidance Goes Only to the Street Corner; the Rest of the Road Is Yours

They passed the first and second guard, and came to the iron gate that led into the city. Luke uses a special word: the gate opened “by itself.” This word appears once in Mark too—“The earth bears fruit of itself” (Mark 4:28); how the seed grows, the sower does not know; it simply grows. How the prison gate opened, Peter did not know; it simply opened.

Then comes a detail easy to overlook: they went out and went along one street, and immediately the angel departed from him. The angel did not accompany him to Mary’s house or plan his next step. The miracle brought him to the street; every step after that depended on his own judgment in the Spirit.

It is like emergency lighting in a building during a blackout—it lights only to the exit and brings you to the street; once in the street, you have to find the way yourself. God’s guidance is often like this: He opens a way for you in the most impossible place but does not walk the whole journey for you.
• Miracles have a boundary: He shows great power where you cannot, and where you can, He wants you responsible.
• From being led to walking on your own: spiritual maturity is still knowing where to go after the angel has left.
IV. “Now I truly know”—Wake Up in the Spirit First, Then Think with the Head

Verse 11 says Peter “came to himself.” He did not first analyze the situation and then believe; he first truly knew in his spirit: this is the Lord sending His angel to rescue me. Only then does verse 12 say that when he had “considered,” he decided to go to Mary’s house.

This order is important: spirit first, understanding afterward. Relying on the Spirit with the heart comes first, using the head to judge comes after; once the heart is aligned with the Lord, the head’s judgment will not be led by fear. That Mary was the mother of John Mark. Her house had an outer gate and a servant girl; it was a fairly large home in the city, and many believe it was where the upper room of the Last Supper was. Peter knew the brothers and sisters were there, because he knew the church would be praying for him.
• The order cannot be reversed: let the heart wake up first, then let the head move; the other way around, the more you think the more afraid you become.
• Know where to go: after danger, the first thing a person of God does is return to the brothers and sisters.
V. “It is his angel”—The People Praying Could Not Believe the Prayer Was Answered

Scene two begins, and the scene is nearly comic. Peter knocked at the door; the servant girl Rhoda (meaning “rose”) came to answer, and on hearing Peter’s voice, in her joy forgot to open the gate and ran in to report. The people inside were praying, and on hearing “Peter is standing outside,” their reaction was: “You are crazy!” When Rhoda insisted, they said: “It is his angel!”—Jews believed each person had a guardian angel who could appear in that person’s likeness. They would rather believe in an angel than dare believe God had really answered their prayer. And Peter? He was outside, “continuing to knock.”

We are often like this too. We pray earnestly yet have not prepared for God really to do it; when God does it, we doubt first and then explain it away with a “spiritual” phrase. God’s work is greater than our faith—this is grace, and also a reminder: He did not wait for our faith to be enough before acting.

When the door opened, they were astonished. Peter motioned to them to be quiet and told “how the Lord had brought him out of the prison”—the subject was the Lord, not himself. He told them to report this to James (the Lord’s brother, by now a leader of the Jerusalem church) and the brothers, and then “departed and went to another place.” He did not stay to receive cheers or turn the miracle into his own stage.
• Prayer must prepare for the answer: if God accomplished it tonight, are you ready to open the door?
• The exit of one emptied of self: the greater the miracle, the more one must learn to step aside and let the Lord receive all the glory.
The Light of the 321 Principles: The Lord’s Hand Is More Real than the Chains

In this passage the most real thing is not the chains, the soldiers, or the iron gate—though all were real; the most real thing is the Lord’s hand. Chains falling off and an iron gate opening by itself were all telling Peter and the church: the One in control is the Lord.

A person of self wants security, so cannot sleep and cannot finish calculating; a person emptied of self wants the Lord, so can sleep soundly even in chains. A person of self, receiving a miracle, turns it into his own capital; a person emptied of self, receiving a miracle, tells “how the Lord brought him,” and having told it, goes to another place.

The Holy Spirit is my guide, but guiding is not replacing. The angel brought Peter to the street corner and left, because what the Lord wants is not a man forever carried but a man who has learned in the Spirit to walk on his own. Building God’s system is exactly like this: not protecting people in a greenhouse but accompanying each person to become an overcomer—able to sleep in chains, able to obey in half-belief, able to know where to go after the angel leaves.
a: Check the Pillow
The matter I say I have entrusted—can I sleep at night? Where I cannot sleep is where I have not let go.
Put On Your Sandals
God breaks the chains; I put on the sandals. Is there something I should do today that I am waiting for God to do in my place?
After the Street Corner
The road after the angel leaves I must walk myself; learn to judge in the Spirit, not only wait for miracles.
Prepare to Open the Door
While praying earnestly, also prepare for God to accomplish it tonight; don’t let God’s answer stand outside knocking.
Tell It and Go
When telling what God has done in me, the subject is the Lord; having told it, I don’t stay in the applause.
q: Is there something now that you said by day you had entrusted to the Lord, yet at night you still toss and turn? What word the Lord had spoken did Peter rely on to sleep between two chains? Do you have a word you can use as a pillow?

The people in Mary’s house prayed earnestly yet could not believe Peter was really standing outside. Recalling your most recent prayer, if God accomplished it today, would you open the door at once or first find a reason to doubt?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that on the night before Herod would bring Peter out, Your angel arrived before Herod. Thank You for letting us see that chains fall off before You and iron gates open by themselves before You; and thank You that when our faith is not enough, You do not therefore refrain from working.
Lord, we confess that we often pray earnestly yet do not prepare for You really to answer; when Your answer comes to the door, we are still inside saying “It is his angel.” Forgive our little faith. Give us sleep like Peter’s, able to place tomorrow in Your hand between the chains; and give us obedient feet, willing after You break the chains to belt up, put on our sandals, and follow. And each time we tell of Your work, may the subject be You, not ourselves. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Now as soon as it was day, there was no small stir among the soldiers about what had become of Peter.
When Herod had sought for him, and didn’t find him, he examined the guards, then commanded that they should be put to death. He went down from Judea to Caesarea, and stayed there.

Now Herod was very angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon. They came with one accord to him, and, having made Blastus, the king’s personal aide, their friend, they asked for peace, because their country depended on the king’s country for food.
On an appointed day, Herod dressed himself in royal clothing, sat on the throne, and gave a speech to them.
The people shouted, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!”
Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, because he didn’t give God the glory. Then he was eaten by worms and died.
But the word of God grew and multiplied.
Barnabas and Saul returned to Jerusalem when they had fulfilled their service, also taking with them John who was called Mark.
b: In the last devotion, Peter left the prison before daybreak, and having told “how the Lord had brought him out of the prison,” went to another place. He made his exit, yet Luke’s camera did not follow him; it stayed in the prison, waiting for daylight.

After daylight, another man’s story comes to its close. This chapter opens with Herod “stretching out his hands” and ends with Herod “giving up the spirit”; in between, one apostle was martyred and one delivered. Luke places all this side by side to make us see one thing: however far man’s hand stretches, the word of God still grows and multiplies.
I. “There was no small stir among the soldiers”—One Night, Two Mornings for Two Kinds of People

Day came. On the church’s side there was astonishment and joy; on the prison’s side, “no small stir.” Roman rules were extremely harsh: if a guard let a prisoner escape, he bore the punishment the prisoner should have borne. So after Herod examined the guards, he ordered them put to death—the very punishment meant to be carried out “before the people” fell on the guards themselves.
Then Herod “went down from Judea to Caesarea.” Caesarea was the seat of the Roman governor, and Herod had his own palace there. Having lost face in Jerusalem, he left the city that embarrassed him.
• The same night, different mornings: those on God’s side received joy; those who controlled by themselves received panic.
• The weakness of power: unable to find one fisherman, he had to kill his own soldiers; the greater a person’s power, the less he can afford to lose.
II. “They came with one accord to him”—The World’s Method: Find Connections, Please People

Verse 20 changes the scene. Herod was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon; these two Phoenician harbor cities depended on Galilee and Judea for their food supply. When Herod cut off the grain, they panicked, and “having made Blastus the king’s chamberlain their friend, they asked for peace.” Blastus was Herod’s chamberlain, in charge of the king’s bedchamber and household affairs, the person closest to the king; the people of Tyre and Sidon went to him and begged him to plead with the king.

This is a typical picture of “how the world works”: those with power apply pressure with grain, and those without power smooth things over through connections. In the whole affair there is no God, only calculation between people.
• The order of self: the world runs on pressure and favors; God’s system runs on letting Jesus be King.
• Which kind is my way: when trouble comes, is my first thought “whom to find” or “find the Lord”?
III. “The voice of a god, and not of a man”—Glory Is the Dividing Line

Verses 21–23 are the climax of this chapter. The Jewish historian Josephus recorded the same event: Herod held a festival for the emperor at Caesarea, and on the second morning entered wearing a robe woven entirely of silver thread; the sunlight struck the robe and it shone so that people could not open their eyes. The flatterers cried out that he was a god, and he did not refuse; at once he was seized with violent stomach pain and died five days later, in AD 44, at the age of fifty-four.

Luke uses just one verse: because he did not give glory to God, an angel of the Lord struck him at once, and he was eaten by worms and died. “An angel of the Lord”—the same angel who struck Peter awake the night before now struck Herod. The angel of God was deliverance in the prison and judgment before the throne.

Note Luke’s diagnosis: not because he killed James, not because he imprisoned Peter; Luke says “because he didn’t give God the glory.” This is exactly the definition of pride: leaving one’s place, grasping power, wanting to replace God. Herod’s problem was not that he was king but that when people cried out “the voice of a god,” he accepted the glory that should have gone to God.

Imagine a glass window. Sunlight passes through it into the room, and those in the room say, “This window is so bright!” If the window thinks the light is its own, at that moment it is no longer a window; the window’s place is to let light pass through. A person’s place is the same: all ability, gifts, and position are for letting God’s glory pass through; the day we keep the light and say “this is mine,” we are standing in Herod’s place.
• Glory is the dividing line: the difference between Herod and Peter is not size of ability but to whom the glory goes.
• Applause is most dangerous: when people cry “the voice of a god” is exactly when one most needs to say “I am not.”
• One’s place is the channel: let God be God and people be people; the light is His, and I am only the window.
IV. “The word of God grew and multiplied”—Worms Ate the King, but the Word Multiplied

Verse 24 is the conclusion of the whole chapter and also a summary sentence Luke habitually uses in the book (6:7 and 9:31 have similar statements). At the beginning of this chapter Herod’s hand reached toward the church; at the end of this chapter Herod was eaten by worms, yet the word of God “grew and multiplied.”

“Grew” in the original is the same as growing, like a plant. However brightly Herod’s robe shone, it was dead matter; the word of God is alive, and when oppressed it grows all the more. James’s blood, Peter’s prison, Herod’s sword—none could stop it.
• A contrasting end: the one in royal robes was eaten by worms; the prisoner lived, and the word lived.
• No need to worry for the word: what we should worry about is never whether the word will flourish but whether I am in the word.
V. “Having fulfilled their service”—Reconnecting the Thread to Antioch

Verse 25 brings the camera back to chapter 11. Barnabas and Saul brought the relief to Jerusalem, “having fulfilled their service,” and returned to Antioch, taking with them John, whose surname was Mark—the John Mark whose mother Mary opened her home for the prayer meeting.

“Service” in the original is “ministry”—a concrete errand of delivering grain. The two who would later open the Gentile mission were at this moment carrying relief supplies, and faithfully “fulfilled” it. What God would send out in the next chapter were exactly these two who were faithful in small things.
• Finish the small thing: first be faithful in delivering grain, then comes the sending of chapter 13.
• Take someone along: on returning they brought a young man; in service, people always matter more than tasks.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Let Jesus Have All the Glory

This passage sets two kinds of life on the same plane: one in royal robes, sitting on the throne, called a god; the other in prison clothes, bound with chains, knocking outside Mary’s door. The former was eaten by worms within five days; the latter lived to testify how the Lord had brought him out of prison. The difference lies in one sentence: to whom the glory goes.

A person of self spends a lifetime collecting glory. When applause comes, he does not refuse it; when others say “the voice of a god,” inwardly he secretly feels it is so. A person emptied of self spends a lifetime sending glory back. When Peter left prison, what he told was “how the Lord brought him,” and having told it, he left. This is not the rhetoric of modesty but the direction of a life: one gathers toward himself, the other sends toward the Lord.

Letting Jesus have all the glory is not deciding whether to give Him glory only after receiving it, but in the very second people cry “the voice of a god,” knowing in the heart at once: that is not me. Humility is the key to revival, because God gives grace to the humble and opposes the proud—Herod was opposed, yet the word multiplied all the more.
a: Two Kinds of Morning
Those who control by themselves receive panic; those on God’s side receive joy; which kind am I this morning?
Find the Lord, Not Connections
In trouble, first ask “What does the Lord say?” not first think “Whom shall I ask to plead?”
Say “Not Me” When Applause Comes
If anyone puts glory on me today, I will send it back at once.
Be the Window, Not the Light
My gifts and position are channels that let God’s glory pass through, not something to keep as my own.
Finish the Small Thing
Like Barnabas and Saul delivering grain, faithfully finish the ordinary task in your hand.
q: “The voice of a god, and not of a man”—in your life, is there a kind of applause or praise you are most reluctant to push away? When it comes, what is your first reaction?

Before being sent, Barnabas and Saul first faithfully completed the errand of delivering grain. What ordinary, unremarkable thing in your hand now, yet given to you by the Lord, have you not yet “fulfilled”?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that this chapter began with Herod’s hand but ended with Your word flourishing. Thank You for letting us see that the one in royal robes on the throne passed in a single night, while Your word grows and multiplies. You are the God who reigns forever.
Lord, Herod’s end makes us tremble. We confess that when applause comes, we too are often reluctant to push it away; when others lift us up, we too secretly feel it is only fitting. Forgive us the heart that steals Your glory. Make us a clean window, letting Your light pass through, keeping not a bit as our own; make us, like Peter, always make You the subject when telling of Your work. And give us a heart faithful in small things, like Barnabas and Saul fulfilling their service, finishing the ordinary errands You put in our hands, to prepare to receive Your next sending. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Now in the assembly that was at Antioch there were some prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen the foster brother of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul.
As they served the Lord and fasted, the Holy Spirit said, “Separate Barnabas and Saul for me, for the work to which I have called them.”
Then, when they had fasted and prayed and laid their hands on them, they sent them away.
b: In the last devotion, Barnabas and Saul fulfilled their service and returned from Jerusalem to Antioch with Mark. Herod was dead, and God’s word spread ever wider.

From this chapter on, Acts opens its second half. The center of the first twelve chapters was Jerusalem and Peter; from here on, the center shifts to Antioch and Paul; the gospel is to go formally from the Jewish world to the ends of the Gentile earth. And a turn this great began not in a strategy meeting but with a group of people hearing the Holy Spirit speak while fasting and worshiping.
I. “Prophets and teachers”—A List That Seems Impossible
Luke lists five names, and the list is itself a sermon.

Barnabas, a Levite from Cyprus, who sold his land and laid it at the apostles’ feet, was the Jerusalem church’s representative sent to Antioch. Simeon who was called Niger—“Niger” is Latin for “black”—was probably a black brother from Africa. Lucius of Cyrene came from Cyrene in North Africa; among those who first preached to the Greeks in Antioch were men of Cyrene (11:20). Manaen, “who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch,” a word meaning foster-brother or childhood playmate—he was raised in the court with Herod Antipas, the Herod who killed John the Baptist. Last was Saul, a Pharisee of Tarsus, formerly the persecutor of the church.

A Levite, an African, a North African, a courtier, a former persecutor. Different skin colors, different classes, different backgrounds, yet serving the Lord together in one church. This was not diversity arranged by design but fruit the gospel naturally bore.

Manaen’s name is especially thought-provoking. Two children raised in the same cradle: one became the tetrarch who killed a prophet, the other became a prophet of the Antioch church. The same start, ends worlds apart, and the difference lay only in who was king in the heart.
• Unity is not sameness: God’s system is not a group of identical people but a group who all let Jesus be King.
• The start does not decide the end: Manaen and Herod were raised together, yet walked entirely different roads; what decides a life is not background but the One on the throne.
II. “As they served the Lord and fasted”—The Sending Happened in Worship

“Served” in verse 2 is a word used originally of priests ministering in the temple, later specifically meaning worship. They were not holding a mission strategy meeting; they were worshiping the Lord and fasting to seek Him. At this very time, the Holy Spirit spoke.

Note the subject: the Holy Spirit said. Not Barnabas proposed, not Saul volunteered, not the church voted. The first impetus of the whole Gentile mission movement was the Spirit’s word. And what the Spirit said was “Separate for me”—for me; “for the work to which I have called them”—I have called. Calling first, sending afterward. Saul had been called by the Lord on the Damascus road to “bear my name before the Gentiles” (9:15), more than ten years earlier; only when the Lord’s time came did the Spirit speak.

Before an orchestra plays, every instrument must first tune to the tuning fork. The Antioch church’s fasting and worship was that tuning—first align oneself with the Lord, and only then can the Spirit’s voice be heard clearly. A person who is never quiet before the Lord often hears only his own thoughts.
• Spirit before understanding: the road of service is spirit, understanding, command, service, God—first the Spirit’s guidance, and then human understanding and action.
• Worship is the seedbed of sending: not first a plan and then asking the Lord to bless it, but first worship, letting the Lord speak.
• The call belongs to the Lord: “I have called them”—the work is the Lord’s, and people are only assigned to do it.
III. “Separate Barnabas and Saul”—The Church Gave Up Its Best Two
The two the Spirit named were Antioch’s two most important coworkers. Barnabas was the church’s founder, Saul its most gifted teacher. Without these two, half of Antioch’s pulpit would be empty.

The church did not bargain, did not say “Can’t You send someone else?” This is giving up self—for Jesus, for others, not for oneself. What the Antioch church gave up was not its leftovers but its best. A mother sending her most beloved child far away, a church sending out its ablest coworkers—both require a center in life truly greater than “me.”
• Give up the best: what God wants is not what I have left over but what I am least willing to give.
• Not for oneself: if a church plans only for its own pulpit, the gospel will never get out of Antioch.
IV. “Fasted and prayed, laid their hands on them, and sent them away”—Letting Go Is the Last Act of Sending

Verse 3 has three actions: fasting and praying, laying on hands, sending away. Fasting and praying was a further confirmation; laying on hands was not conferring power but declaring identification—when you go, we go, and we are with you. “Sent away” in the original is “released”: loosening the hand, letting them go. Verse 4 immediately says “So they, being sent out by the Holy Spirit”—the church released, the Holy Spirit sent.

For a bow to shoot an arrow, it must first be drawn and then released. Fasting and prayer is drawing the bow, laying on hands is aiming, sending away is letting go. If the bow cannot bear to let go, the arrow stays on the string forever. The Antioch church drew the bow fully and then released, and so the arrow flew to Cyprus, to Asia Minor, to Europe, and to this day has reached us.
• The church is the bow, not the arrow: our duty is to draw fully, to aim, and then to let go; where the arrow goes is the Spirit’s business.
• Letting go is an act of faith: what grips is self; what loosens is handing people to the Lord.
The Light of the 321 Principles: The Holy Spirit Is My Guide

The second half of Acts begins with three words: the Holy Spirit said. In the whole Gentile mission, not one step was initiated by people first—the Spirit spoke in worship, the Spirit named, the Spirit sent. All the Antioch church did was be quiet before the Lord, hear, and obey.

A person of self is used to making a plan first and then asking the Lord to bless it, so the Spirit’s guidance becomes one of many opinions. A person emptied of self first fasts and worships, brings himself to zero, and lets the Lord speak. The reason the Antioch church could hear the Spirit was that it was while they were serving the Lord and fasting—when they had set themselves down.

This is also the pattern of building God’s system: not by connections and organization but by a group of people who let Jesus be King, guided by the Spirit in worship, and then willing to give up their best. A system is not for keeping people but for sending people; not for enlarging itself but for letting the gospel reach the ends of the earth. The arrow shot from Antioch has flown two thousand years and is still flying today.
a: How I See Coworkers
Not by background, skin color, or past, but by whether in his heart he lets Jesus be King.
Worship Before Planning
For today’s decision, first be quiet before the Lord and tune, don’t first use the head.
The Call Belongs to the Lord
The ministry in my hand was called by the Lord, it is the Lord’s work, and I am only the one assigned.
Give Up the Best
Ask myself: if the Lord wants the one thing I am least willing to give, will I give it?
Learn to Let Go
For the people I am nurturing and the ministry I treasure, can I draw the bow fully and then loosen my hand?
q: The Antioch church heard the Spirit speak “as they served the Lord and fasted.” Recall a major decision you recently made: did you first become quiet before the Lord, or first calculate with your head? Was there room in it for the Spirit to speak?
The church gave up its best, Barnabas and Saul. Is there a person, a ministry, or a resource in your life that you would be unwilling to let go of if the Lord wanted it? What holds you back?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that the first step of the Gentile mission was not thought up by people but spoken by the Spirit. Thank You for gathering in Antioch a Levite, Africans, a courtier, and a former persecutor, letting them serve You together, so that we may see what Your system looks like.
Lord, we confess that we often make a plan first and then ask You to bless it, leaving Your guidance last. Teach us, like the Antioch church, to serve You first, to fast first, to bring ourselves to zero first, and only then listen to You speak. Give us a heart that is willing to give, to give up the best, not planning for our own pulpit; and give us the faith to let go, willing after drawing the bow fully to loosen our hand, so that Your arrow flies where You want it to go. May the Holy Spirit speak among us also, and may we obey when we hear. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia. From there they sailed to Cyprus.
When they were at Salamis, they proclaimed God’s word in the Jewish synagogues. They also had John as their attendant.
When they had gone through the island to Paphos, they found a certain sorcerer, a false prophet, a Jew, whose name was Bar Jesus,
who was with the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, a man of understanding. This man summoned Barnabas and Saul, and sought to hear the word of God.
But Elymas the sorcerer (for so is his name by interpretation) withstood them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith.
But Saul, who is also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, fastened his eyes on him,
and said, “You son of the devil, full of all deceit and all cunning, you enemy of all righteousness, will you not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord?

Now, behold, the hand of the Lord is on you, and you will be blind, not seeing the sun for a season!” Immediately a mist and darkness fell on him. He went around seeking someone to lead him by the hand.
Then the proconsul, when he saw what was done, believed, being astonished at the teaching of the Lord.
b: In the last devotion, the Antioch church heard the Holy Spirit speak in fasting and worship, laid hands on Barnabas and Saul, and sent them out. The bow was fully drawn, and the hand loosened.

Today the arrow has flown. The first stop is Cyprus. In this passage Luke lets us see two things: the first time the gospel formally set foot on Gentile soil, it met opposition; and in this encounter, “Saul” was for the first time called “Paul.” From then on Luke never calls him Saul again.
I. “Being sent out by the Holy Spirit”—Beginning in the Most Familiar Place
Verse 4 stresses once more: they were sent out by the Holy Spirit. The church sent, the Spirit sent out; people’s hands let go, God’s hand caught.

They went down to Seleucia, Antioch’s seaport about fifteen miles away, and from there sailed to Cyprus. Why Cyprus? Because it was Barnabas’s homeland (4:36). The Spirit did not send them to the most unfamiliar place but first to the most familiar. Salamis was a large city on the island’s east coast with many Jews and more than one synagogue, so Luke says “the synagogues of the Jews.” Their strategy was clear: first to the Jewish synagogues, because the people there already had the Scriptures, the promises, and hearts waiting for the Messiah.
John Mark was their “attendant,” a word for an assistant who handled the odd jobs, arranging the itinerary and looking after daily needs. A young man begins as an assistant.
• Begin in the familiar: God’s sending often first lands where you are already standing.
• Being an assistant is also service: Mark began with odd jobs and later wrote a Gospel.
II. “A Jewish false prophet, whose name was Bar-Jesus”—When the True Word Arrives, the False Is Exposed

They crossed the whole island, about a hundred miles, and came to Paphos on the west coast, seat of the Roman proconsul and also the center of worship of the goddess Aphrodite. Here they met a man whom Luke describes with three words: sorcerer, false prophet, Jew. His name was Bar-Jesus, meaning “son of Jesus (Joshua)”—a fraud carrying the Savior’s name. He was also called Elymas, which Luke explains means “sorcerer.”

He “was with the proconsul, Sergius Paulus.” The proconsul was the provincial governor; Cyprus was then a senatorial province governed by a proconsul, and Luke’s word is exactly right. Sergius Paulus was “a man of understanding,” a Roman nobleman with a mind who was willing to think; keeping a sorcerer by his side was the fashion of high society then. This governor, hearing that someone was preaching the word of God, sent for Barnabas and Saul and wanted to hear.

Elymas was alarmed. If the governor believed the true word, the sorcerer’s livelihood would be gone. So he “withstood them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith.” This is a picture ever new: when the true word arrives, those who live on a false one rise up to block it—not because he does not know it is true, but because once the true comes, his position is gone.
• The false fears the true most: Elymas’s motive for opposing was to protect his own position.
• Looking at faith through “self”: whoever in faith first asks “What about my position?” has the same heart as Elymas.
III. “Saul, who also is called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, fixed his eyes on him”—The Name Changed, the Lordship Did Not

Verse 9 is a watershed. Here Luke writes for the first time “Saul, who is also called Paul,” and from then on the whole book uses only the name Paul. Paul was his Roman name, meaning “small”; Saul was his Hebrew name, the name of Israel’s first king. As the gospel went toward the Gentile world, he used the name of the Gentile world; one called “small” would carry the One who is “great” to the nations.

“Filled with the Holy Spirit”—Luke notes specially that what Paul said next was not his temper but the Spirit’s word. He “fixed his eyes on him,” looking straight at Elymas, and said the sternest sentence of his life: “You son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, full of all deceit and all unscrupulousness.” Bar-Jesus, “son of Jesus,” was named “son of the devil.” The name was false; the identity was real.

“Perverting the right ways of the Lord” in the original is making straight paths crooked. Isaiah said to “make straight in the desert a highway for our God” (Isaiah 40:3); Satan’s work is the opposite, bending the straight road. It is like someone turning a signpost at a junction—the sign is still there, the words unchanged, but it points down the wrong road. A false way never takes truth away; it twists it a little.
• The name changed, the lordship did not: from Saul to Paul, what changed was the outward name; what did not change was the King in the heart.
• Discernment depends on the Spirit: Elymas was “false,” not visible to the naked eye; only one filled with the Holy Spirit could fix his eyes and see through.
IV. “You will be blind, not seeing the sun for a season”—A Judgment Paul Understood Best

The Lord’s hand came on Elymas, and he went blind, “seeking someone to lead him by the hand.” This picture Paul knew all too well—more than ten years earlier on the Damascus road he himself had gone blind, and “they led him by the hand and brought him into Damascus” (9:8).

So notice the phrase: “for a season.” This was not an eternal judgment but temporary darkness. Paul knew there is a kind of darkness for the purpose of letting a person see. He himself, in three days of darkness, saw the Lord he had been persecuting. Mercy hides inside God’s judgment; He strikes in order to heal.
• Mercy within judgment: the words “for a season” were a door left for Elymas.
• Seeing others from one’s own darkness: Paul’s way of dealing with an enemy carried the memory of his own having received grace.
V. “Being astonished at the teaching of the Lord, believed”—The Governor Believed Not in the Miracle but in the Word

Verse 12 says the proconsul “saw what was done,” but Luke goes on to say that what astonished him was “the teaching of the Lord,” and then he believed. The miracle opened his eyes, and the word entered his heart. A man of understanding was in the end persuaded by truth, not frightened into submission by wonders.
This was the first fruit of the Gentile mission: a Roman governor. The first step of the gospel into the Gentile world took a stand in the very center of Roman power.
• The miracle is the signpost; the word is the destination: people are astonished when they see wonders, but what truly saves is the word.
• People of understanding also need the word: intelligence is not the obstacle; pride is.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Self-Denial Overcomes Satan

This confrontation at Paphos was the first head-on contest in Acts between the gospel and sorcery. Paul won, but how he won is worth a close look: not by eloquence, not by his own authority, but by being “filled with the Holy Spirit.”

A person of self, fighting Satan, uses his own flesh and blood, and the result is that the harder he fights, the more he looks like his opponent. A person emptied of self, fighting Satan, lets the Holy Spirit fill him and lets the Lord’s hand come on the other—the subject is the Lord, not Paul. “Now, behold, the hand of the Lord is on you,” not “my hand.” Elymas perverted the Lord’s right ways because in his heart he was king of himself; Paul exposed him because in Paul’s heart there was no longer a self.

The focus is on Jesus, not on myself, not on others, not on circumstances. From Saul to Paul the name changed, but this did not. When a person is truly emptied of self, Satan finds no place to lay hold—because all of Satan’s tricks are aimed at that “self”: making you afraid of losing your position, making you protect your livelihood, making you care how you look. Elymas fell here, and Paul’s victory lay here too.
a: Begin Where I Stand
God’s sending first lands on familiar people and things; no need to wait for far places.
Examine My Opposition
My resistance to some truth—is it because it threatens my position?
Discern by the Spirit
A false way bends a straight road just a little; only one filled with the Holy Spirit can see through it.
Remember My Own Darkness
When dealing with someone in error, carry the memory of having received mercy, and leave a “for a season” door open.
Let the Lord’s Hand Work
In contending with darkness, don’t use my flesh and blood; let the Lord’s hand come upon it.
q: Elymas opposed the true word because it threatened his position. Think honestly: is there a truth you have never been willing to accept? What of yours does it threaten?

Paul said “for a season” of the blindness because he remembered his own three days of darkness at Damascus. When you face someone plainly in error, does your attitude contain a “for a season”—the mercy of leaving a door open?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that as soon as the arrow was shot there was fruit. Thank You that the first time the gospel set foot on Gentile soil it bore fruit in a Roman governor; and thank You for letting us see that when the true word arrives, the false has nowhere to hide.
Lord, we confess there is a shadow of Elymas in us too—when truth threatens our position, our face, our livelihood, we also rise up to block it. Forgive us. Fill us with the Holy Spirit, so that we have eyes that fix and see through, able to discern signposts twisted just a little; and make us remember our own former darkness, still carrying mercy when dealing with error. May every one of our contests be not by our own flesh and blood but by letting Your hand work; may a change like that from Saul to Paul happen in us too—the name may change, but that You are King in our hearts will never change. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Now Paul and his company set sail from Paphos, and came to Perga in Pamphylia. John departed from them and returned to Jerusalem.
But they, passing on from Perga, came to Antioch of Pisidia. They went into the synagogue on the Sabbath day, and sat down.
After the reading of the law and the prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent to them, saying, “Brothers, if you have any word of exhortation for the people, speak.”
Paul stood up, and beckoning with his hand said, “Men of Israel, and you who fear God, listen.
The God of this people chose our fathers, and exalted the people when they stayed as aliens in the land of Egypt, and with an uplifted arm, he led them out of it.
For a period of about forty years he put up with them in the wilderness.
When he had destroyed seven nations in the land of Canaan, he gave them their land for an inheritance for about four hundred fifty years.
After these things, he gave them judges until Samuel the prophet.
Afterward they asked for a king, and God gave to them Saul the son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years.
When he had removed him, he raised up David to be their king, to whom he also testified, ‘I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after my heart, who will do all my will.’
From this man’s offspring, God has brought salvation to Israel according to his promise,
before his coming, when John had first preached the baptism of repentance to Israel.
As John was fulfilling his course, he said, ‘What do you suppose that I am? I am not he. But behold, one comes after me, the sandals of whose feet I am not worthy to untie.’
b: In the last devotion, the gospel won its first confrontation at Paphos, the Roman governor believed in the Lord, and from then on Saul was called Paul.

Today the company leaves Cyprus, lands on the mainland of Asia Minor, and heads for the interior plateau. Luke first records one man’s departure and then the opening of a sermon. This is the first complete sermon of Paul recorded in Acts; he begins from Abraham and goes all the way to Jesus. Today we hear the first half—a history in which God is the subject.
I. “John departed from them and returned to Jerusalem”—A Young Man Drops Out Midway

Sailing from Paphos, they came to Perga in Pamphylia, a city on the south coast of Asia Minor. It was here that “John departed from them and returned to Jerusalem.” Luke writes only this one sentence and gives no reason.

Perhaps the route had changed: now they had to cross the Taurus Mountains by a path haunted by bandits and malarial air; perhaps the leadership had changed: verse 13 writes “Paul and his company” for the first time, so the one in the lead had changed from Barnabas (his cousin) to Paul; perhaps he could not accept the gospel going so directly toward Gentiles. In any case, he went home. The aftereffects were great: later Paul quarreled with Barnabas over this and they separated (15:38–39).

But the story did not stop there. Many years later, Paul wrote from prison to Timothy: “Take Mark, and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service” (2 Timothy 4:11). The young man who dropped out midway later wrote the Gospel of Mark.
• Dropping out is not the end: one weakness is not an eternal label in God’s hands.
• How I see those who drop out: Barnabas later gave Mark another chance; toward a fallen brother, do I condemn or accompany?
II. “They sat down on the Sabbath day in the synagogue”—They Entered a House Waiting for the Messiah

Leaving Perga, they traveled about a hundred miles of mountain road to Antioch of Pisidia. This city, over three thousand feet above sea level, was a Roman colony and a major city of the province of Galatia, with the same name as the Syrian Antioch that had sent them out.

On the Sabbath they went into the synagogue and sat down. The synagogue service had a fixed order: reciting the Shema, prayer, reading the Law, reading the Prophets, and then a learned man gave a word of exhortation. The synagogue rulers, in charge of arranging speakers, seeing two visitors from afar, sent word to them: “Brothers, if you have any word of exhortation for the people, speak.”

Paul stood up and “motioned with his hand”—the gesture with which a Greek orator began. His opening addressed two kinds of hearers: “Men of Israel” and “you who fear God.” The latter were Gentiles drawn to Israel’s God who came to worship in the synagogue but had not formally joined Judaism. From his first words, Paul counted this group in.
• Preach from the foundation already there: first speak to those with the Scriptures in hand and waiting in their hearts.
• Don’t leave out those at the door: Paul’s first sentence named “you who fear God”; when I speak, do my eyes include those standing at the door, not yet inside?
III. “God chose… exalted… brought them out… put up with… gave… gave judges”—A History with God as the Subject

In verses 17–20 Paul went through nearly five hundred years of Israel’s history with a series of verbs, and the subject of every verb was God: God chose the fathers, God exalted them, God brought them out with an uplifted arm, God put up with them in the wilderness for forty years, God destroyed seven nations in Canaan and gave them the land, God gave them judges. “About four hundred fifty years” is the sum from the sojourn in Egypt to the allotting of the land.

Verse 18’s “put up with” has a variant reading, differing by a single letter, meaning “cared for”—like a father carrying a child. Put side by side, the two words fit exactly the forty years in the wilderness: God bore with their rebellion on one hand and carried them through on the other.

Looking at a river from downstream, you see only the water passing before your eyes; only from a height do you see where it came from and where it is going. Paul took the congregation up to the height to let them see: your history is not a string of accidents but God’s step-by-step work. Israel was only the one chosen, brought out, cared for, and settled.
• See myself from God’s viewpoint: in my past, is the subject God or me?
• Bearing with and carrying: God puts up with my rebellion and at the same time carries me through the wilderness; He has always done both at once.
IV. “Afterward they asked for a king”—The King People Asked For and the King God Chose

Verse 21 gives the first action with people as the subject: “They asked for a king.” God gave them Saul the son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin, who reigned forty years. Then God removed Saul and raised up David.

There is a detail worth noting: the preacher was himself named Saul, and also of the tribe of Benjamin (Romans 11:1). He stood in the synagogue and spoke of how a king with his own name and tribe was removed.
