He did not avoid it, because this was exactly what he meant: the king people ask for themselves will be removed; the king God chooses for Himself is the one who fits His heart.

“A man after my heart, who will do all my will”—David fit God’s heart not because he never sinned but because the direction of his life was to do God’s will, and when he fell he returned to God. Fitting God’s heart is not perfection but obedience.
• The king people ask for is removed: if in my heart I have set up a “king” of my own choosing—reputation, security, being affirmed—it will not stand in the end.
• Fitting His heart means obedience: not never falling, but, having fallen, still taking doing God’s will as the direction of life.
V. “God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus”—John’s Self-Denial Paved the Way for That One
Verse 23: history arrived at its destination—from David’s offspring, according to promise, God brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus. Five hundred years of history, every verb, was to reach this name.

Paul then mentioned John the Baptist, because John’s fame at that time had reached the synagogues everywhere. As John was “fulfilling his course,” he said two things: “I am not he”; “I am not worthy to loosen the sandals of his feet.” Loosening sandal straps was the lowliest work of a household slave; rabbis even ruled that a Hebrew slave could refuse to do it. John said he was not worthy even of that.

John knew who he was and also who he was not. This is self-denial: not belittling oneself but putting oneself back in place—he was the forerunner, not the main figure; his work was to point people’s eyes to the One coming after him.
• Know who I am not: “I am not he”—this sentence should still be said often in the heart today.
• Let that One receive the glory: when John finished his course, what people remembered was not him but the Jesus he pointed to.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Changing from a Human Viewpoint to God’s Viewpoint

Paul’s sermon is a lesson in “changing viewpoint.” The same stretch of history, from a human viewpoint, is the rise and fall of Israel; from God’s viewpoint, it is God’s choosing, bringing out, caring for, settling, and promising. When the subject changes, the whole story changes.

A person of self reads his own life with the subject always “I”: I worked hard, I succeeded, I was wronged, I didn’t get it. A person emptied of self reads his own life with the subject God: He chose, He led, He bore with, He cared for. Change your concepts and you change your life; change your life and you change your daily living—when the subject changes from “I” to “God,” anxiety turns into thanksgiving and complaint turns into worship.

And the end of history is a name: Jesus. The king people asked for was removed; the King God chose stood. John paved the way for Him with “I am not he.” Letting Jesus be King, viewed from history, is acknowledging that this whole river, from beginning to end, flows toward Him.
a: Leave a Road for Those Who Drop Out
One weakness is not an eternal label; toward the fallen I should be like Barnabas.
Keep the Door in View
When speaking, remember those who “fear God” but have not yet come in.
Read My Life with a New Subject
Today reread my past with the subject changed to God—He chose, He led, He cared for.
Remove the King I Chose
Examine what king I have set up in my heart, and hand it over.
Often Say “I Am Not”
Like John, know I am not the main figure, and point my eyes to the One coming after.
q: Try retelling your journey since believing, with God as the subject: “God chose me… God brought me out… God put up with me in the wilderness…” Write three sentences. After retelling it this way, how does your heart feel differently?
“They asked for a king”—is there a king in your heart that you asked for yourself? In what matters does it keep you from “doing all God’s will”?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that You are the subject of history. You chose, You brought out, You bore with and cared for in the wilderness, You gave the land, You raised up a king, and according to promise You brought a Savior, Jesus. Thank You for letting us see that our whole lives also lie in Your hand, not a string of accidents.
Lord, we confess that when we read our own lives the subject is often “I”; we also often ask for a king of our own, setting reputation, security, and being affirmed on the throne of our hearts. Remove the kings we set up, and let the One You chose be King in our hearts. Teach us, like John, to know who we are and who we are not, able often to say “I am not the Christ,” and to point all eyes to You. And give us the heart of Barnabas, to leave a road back for those who drop out midway. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Brothers, children of the stock of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, the word of this salvation is sent out to you.
For those who dwell in Jerusalem, and their rulers, because they didn’t know him, nor the voices of the prophets which are read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning him.
Though they found no cause for death, they still asked Pilate to have him killed.
When they had fulfilled all things that were written about him, they took him down from the tree, and laid him in a tomb.
But God raised him from the dead,
and he was seen for many days by those who came up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are his witnesses to the people.
We bring you good news of the promise made to the fathers,
that God has fulfilled this to us, their children, in that he raised up Jesus. As it is also written in the second psalm, ‘You are my Son. Today I have become your father.’
b: In the last devotion, in the synagogue of Antioch of Pisidia, Paul told Israel’s five hundred years of history as a book with God as its subject, all the way to “God brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus,” and had John the Baptist testify to Him: “I am not he.”

Today the sermon moves to its second part. Paul changes his tone, addresses his hearers again, and then turns the focus from history to what had happened in Jerusalem only a few weeks before: how that Savior was condemned, killed, and buried, and how God raised Him from the dead. The watershed of the whole passage is verse 30, one short sentence: “But God raised him from the dead.”
I. “To us is the word of this salvation sent out”—Naming Them a Second Time, Counting the Gentiles in “Us”

Verse 26: Paul opens again with a new form of address: “Brothers, children of the stock of Abraham, and those among you who fear God.” As in verse 16, he sets Jews and God-fearing Gentiles side by side, and then says: the word of this salvation was sent out to “us.”

“Us”—not to your forefathers, nor to Jerusalem, but to us who are sitting here, including those Gentiles at the door who had not yet joined Judaism. Salvation is not news from far away; it is a letter delivered to you.
• The word is sent to “me”: reading the Bible is not reading someone else’s history but reading a letter addressed to myself.
• Gentiles are in the “us”: Paul counted those at the door in a second time; in God’s system there is no spectators’ gallery.
II. “Because they didn’t know him, and the voices of the prophets which are read every Sabbath”—Read Every Week, Yet Not Understood

Verse 27 is a grievous diagnosis. Those who lived in Jerusalem and their rulers condemned the Christ to death because “they didn’t know him, and the voices of the prophets which are read every Sabbath.”

Note: it was not that they had not read. Every Sabbath the prophets were read aloud in the synagogue, and they had heard them all their lives. But they did not understand. More ironic still, their not understanding “fulfilled” the prophets—by not understanding the prophets, they fulfilled the prophets.

It is like a man who passes the same junction on his way to work every day, where a signpost stands; he has walked it for twenty years yet never once looked up at what the sign says. Being familiar is not knowing, and having read is not understanding. And the place where Paul said this was exactly a synagogue where “the prophets are read every Sabbath”; he was warning the group before him: Jerusalem’s mistake could be yours too.
• Reading Scripture means meeting Christ: the Bible is my standard, but the center of the standard is a living Lord; if I read for a long time without meeting Him, I still “don’t know.”
• Familiarity is the greatest danger: the more familiar the passage, the more one should look up once to see whom it is talking about.
III. “Though they found no cause for death in him, they asked of Pilate that he should be killed”—The Innocent One Really Died

Verses 28–29: Paul covered the cross in the briefest words: though they found no cause for death, they asked Pilate to kill Him; when they had fulfilled all that was written, they took Him down from the tree and laid Him in a tomb.

The word “tree” is deliberate. Deuteronomy says, “he who is hanged is accursed of God” (Deuteronomy 21:23). Later in Galatians Paul quotes this, saying Christ became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). This man in whom no guilt was found was hung on a tree and bore the curse. Then “laid in a tomb”—He did not faint; He truly died and was truly buried. The resurrection is a resurrection because death was first real.
The whole series of verbs is human action: condemn, ask, kill, take down, lay in a tomb. People did everything they could do and finished Him off completely.
• He bore the curse for me: the One on the tree was without sin; the sinner is I standing under the tree.
• Human hands went all the way: people condemned Him, killed Him, buried Him; people thought it was over.
IV. “But God raised him from the dead”—A Whole Series of Human Actions Turned Over by One Act of God

Verse 30 is only a few words, yet it is the pivot of the whole sermon. People did so much—but God raised Him from the dead. This “but” is the same kind of turn as the “but” of chapter 12, “Peter was kept in the prison, but constant prayer was being made by the assembly”: where people’s hands stop, God’s hand begins.

Paul then brought in the witnesses: “those who came up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are his witnesses to the people.” He was honest—he himself was not among that group; he was not a disciple who had come up from Galilee. What he preached could be checked: those people were still alive, right among the people.
• Man’s ending is God’s beginning: when you think the matter has been “laid in the tomb,” remember there is still a “but.”
• Testimony can be checked: the gospel stands on living witnesses, not on the speaker’s eloquence.
V. “We bring you good news”—The Promise Was Not Delayed but Fulfilled

Verses 32–33: Paul spoke the words “good news”—the gospel. What was its content? “That God has fulfilled this to our children, in that he raised up Jesus.” The fathers received the promise; our generation received the fulfillment.

Then he quoted Psalm 2: “You are my Son. Today I have become your father.” This was a psalm used at the enthronement of Israel’s kings. “Today I have become your father” does not mean Jesus became God’s Son only on that day, but that on the day of the resurrection He was publicly installed as King, as Paul later wrote in Romans: “who was declared to be the Son of God with power… by the resurrection from the dead” (Romans 1:4). The resurrection was not just coming back to life; it was an enthronement.
• The promise is fulfilled: we do not live in waiting but in accomplishment.
• Resurrection is enthronement: letting Jesus be King is not our decision but a fact God declared on the day of the resurrection.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Changing from a Human Viewpoint to God’s Viewpoint—“But”

Two viewpoints collide in this passage. From the human viewpoint, the story ended at verse 29: condemned, killed, buried, an innocent man disposed of, the prophets read every week as before, nothing changed. From God’s viewpoint, verse 30 is the center of the story: but God raised Him from the dead.

A person of self lives in verse 29. He sees only what people did—how others treated me, how circumstances treated me, how the matter was buried; he reads the prophets every week yet never looks up to see the Lord. A person emptied of self lives in verse 30. He knows that where people’s hands stop, God’s hand begins; he reads the same book yet meets Christ on every page.

Change your concepts and you change your life: move the eyes from “they laid Him in a tomb” to “but God raised Him,” from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal. On the day of the resurrection, the Father said to the Son, “You are my Son,” and He was enthroned. To let Jesus be King is to move the center of life from verse 29 to verse 30.
a: Read the Letter as Written to Me
This word of salvation was sent to “me”; when reading Scripture today, remember the recipient is myself.
Look Up at the Signpost
The most familiar passage—ask once more today whom it is really pointing to.
Stand Under the Tree
Remember the One hanging is without sin and the sinner is I; He bore the curse for me.
Remember That “But”
When a matter seems buried, God’s hand is just about to begin; don’t stop at verse 29.
Acknowledge That He Is Enthroned
Resurrection is enthronement; today let Him truly be King in my heart.
q: The people of Jerusalem had the prophets “read every Sabbath” yet “didn’t know” Him. Is there a passage you know so well that you no longer ask whom it is talking about? Reread it today: do you see Christ?
Is there something in your life you have “laid in the tomb”—decided it was over, hopeless? What does the sentence “But God raised him from the dead” mean for that matter?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that the word of this salvation was sent to us—not news from far away but a letter delivered to us. Thank You that though people condemned Your Son, killed Him, and laid Him in a tomb, You raised Him from the dead; where people’s hands stop, Your hand begins.
Lord, we confess that we are often like the people of Jerusalem, reading the prophets every Sabbath yet not knowing You, opening the Bible every day yet not looking up to see You. Forgive our familiarity and numbness, and let us meet You on every page of Scripture. Move also the center of our lives from verse 29 to verse 30—from how people treat me to what You have done; from the tomb to the resurrection. You were enthroned as King on the day of the resurrection; be King in our hearts today as well. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: “Concerning that he raised him up from the dead, now no more to return to corruption, he has spoken thus: ‘I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David.’
Therefore he says also in another psalm, ‘You will not allow your Holy One to see decay.’
For David, after he had in his own generation served the counsel of God, fell asleep, was laid with his fathers, and saw decay.
But he whom God raised up saw no decay.
Be it known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man is proclaimed to you remission of sins,
and by him everyone who believes is justified from all things, from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses.
Beware therefore, lest that come on you which is spoken in the prophets:
‘Behold, you scoffers, and wonder, and perish; for I work a work in your days, a work which you will in no way believe, if one declares it to you.’ ”
b: In the last devotion, Paul’s sermon stopped on the “but” of verse 30: people laid Him in a tomb, but God raised Him from the dead; and he quoted Psalm 2, declaring that the resurrection is an enthronement—“You are my Son. Today I have become your father.”

Today is the close of this sermon. Paul has three things to do: prove from Scripture that the resurrected One will not decay, proclaim the word of forgiveness and justification, and finally give a stern warning. The whole sermon began with history but stops at a decision: believe, or scorn.
I. “No more to return to corruption”—Two Verses Proving That the Resurrected One Will Not Die Again

Verses 34–35: Paul quoted two passages. One was from Isaiah: “I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David” (Isaiah 55:3); the other from Psalm 16: “You will not allow your Holy One to see decay” (Psalm 16:10).

In the original these two share one word—“holy” and “Holy One” come from the same root. This was a method of interpretation common among Jewish rabbis: when two passages share a word, they can interpret each other. Paul’s logic: the grace God promised David is “sure” and will never come to nothing; and for it never to come to nothing, the “Holy One” who receives the promise must “not see decay”—He cannot die and stay dead. A Savior who decays cannot bring sure grace.

“No more to return to corruption”—this is where it differs from the resurrection of Lazarus. Lazarus lived and later died again; Jesus lived and lives forever. For the first time, death was thoroughly nullified.
• Why grace is sure: because the Lord who bears the grace will not die again; what I trust in does not expire.
• Read Scripture seeing the connections: the Bible is my standard, and the standard is a whole book whose parts confirm each other.
II. “David… saw decay; but he whom God raised up saw no decay”—One Tomb Full, One Empty

Verses 36–37: Paul’s argument is exactly the same as Peter’s at Pentecost (2:29–31): Psalm 16 cannot be David speaking of himself, because David “saw decay,” and his tomb is still in Jerusalem. So the Holy One who “saw no decay” can only be another—the One God raised up.

But here Paul added a very beautiful line describing David’s life: “For David, after he had in his own generation served the counsel of God, fell asleep.” This is the best summary of a person’s life: he served his own generation and then fell asleep. David did not outlive his generation; he simply looked after his own generation well.
• Two tombs: the greatest king is still in the grave, and our Lord has come out; faith stands on this difference.
• Serve the people of this generation: I need not change history, only serve according to God’s will the generation God has placed me in.
III. “Through this man is proclaimed to you remission of sins”—What the Law Could Not Do, This One Did

Verses 38–39 are the core declaration of the whole sermon. “Be it known to you therefore, brothers.” Paul used “this man” twice—through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you; in this man everyone who believes is justified.

“Forgiveness” in the original is “release,” a debt wiped out. “Justified” is a courtroom term, the judge’s declaration: not guilty, righteous. Paul said it directly: “from which you couldn’t be justified by the law of Moses”—the law has things it cannot do. The law can tell you what sin is but cannot remove sin; it can condemn you but cannot declare you not guilty. And “in this one everyone who believes is justified.”

The law is like a bill that lists every item you owe clearly. The bill is accurate, but the bill does not pay for you; the more carefully you read it, the more you know you cannot pay. Justification is not the bill torn up, but someone paying it off for you, and then the judge declares: this person owes nothing. This is exactly what Paul repeated later in Romans and Galatians, and Luke lets us hear that this principle was first spoken in a synagogue, to Jews and God-fearing Gentiles.
• Admit you cannot be justified: the entrance to justification is first admitting that before the law I truly cannot; this step is hardest for people of self.
• Trust this man: not trusting how well I keep the law, but trusting the One who paid it off for me.
IV. “Beware”—The Scornful Cannot See What God Is Doing

Verses 40–41: Paul closed by quoting Habakkuk (Habakkuk 1:5). In that day God said to Judah: I am raising up the Chaldeans, a work “which you will in no way believe, though someone declare it to you.” God was doing something, yet because of scorn, people would not believe it no matter what.

Paul pointed these words at the congregation before him: in your days God has done a work—raising Jesus from the dead—and now someone has declared it to you; beware lest you become one of the “scoffers.” To scoff is to treat what God has done as of no account; not fierce opposition, only feeling it does not matter. Paul knew that what hinders people from believing is often not opposition but indifference.
This is a stern warning, yet it comes from love. If a doctor sees a disease and does not say so, that is not gentleness but dereliction.
• Indifference is more dangerous than opposition: unbelief is often not fierce opposition but only “whatever.”
• A warning is love: a word that truly loves people states the consequences plainly.
The Light of the 321 Principles: God Gives Grace to the Humble and Opposes the Proud

The close of this sermon sets two kinds of people before us: those who “trust in this one in everything the law could not justify,” and the “scoffers.” The former are justified, the latter will perish. Where is the difference? In whether one admits he cannot.

Pride is leaving one’s place and wanting to replace God; in the matter of justification, pride looks like “I can keep the law by myself.” Humility is returning to one’s place, letting God be God and people be people; humility looks like admitting: I cannot pay the bill; I need that One to pay for me. God gives grace to the humble and opposes the proud—not that God plays favorites, but that the proud simply will not reach out to receive.

Self-denial is not having nothing but entering the limitless. Admitting “I cannot be justified” looks like loss but is in fact entering the holy, sure grace given by the Lord who is “no more to return to corruption.” David served his own generation and then fell asleep; we too need only, in our own generation, not be scoffers but be those who trust this man.
a: Trust the Lord Who Does Not Expire
Of all I rely on, only the One who no longer decays is sure.
Serve My Generation
No need to change history, only serve according to God’s will those among whom God has placed me.
Admit I Cannot Pay the Bill
Be honest today: in what matters am I still relying on keeping things well myself?
Trust Only This Man
Justification is not by how well I do but by His having paid it off for me.
Don’t Be a Scoffer
Of what God is doing today, don’t say “whatever.”
q: “From which you couldn’t be justified by the law of Moses”—is there something you still secretly feel is “I keep it well enough, so God should accept me”? If that could not in fact justify you, how would you see yourself?

“David, after he had in his own generation served the counsel of God, fell asleep.” If your whole life could be summed up in one sentence, what would you want it to be? Does that sentence match the direction of your daily life now?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that the grace You promised David is holy and sure, because the Lord who bears this grace has been raised and will no more return to corruption. Thank You that through this man the word of forgiveness is proclaimed to us, and in all that the law could not justify, those who trust Him are all justified.
Lord, we confess that there is still pride in us, always wanting to keep things a little better ourselves so as to stand before You; we also confess that we are often scornful and indifferent toward what You are doing. Forgive us. Bring us back to our place, to admit honestly that we cannot pay the bill, and to trust in You alone; and make us, like David, serve according to Your will the people of our generation, and then sleep peacefully in Your arms. May we not be scoffers but those who trust this man. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: So when the Jews went out of the synagogue, the Gentiles begged that these words might be preached to them the next Sabbath.
Now when the synagogue broke up, many of the Jews and of the devout proselytes followed Paul and Barnabas; who, speaking to them, urged them to continue in the grace of God.
The next Sabbath, almost the whole city was gathered together to hear the word of God.
But when the Jews saw the multitudes, they were filled with jealousy, and contradicted the things which were spoken by Paul, and blasphemed.

Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly, and said, “It was necessary that God’s word should be spoken to you first. Since indeed you thrust it from yourselves, and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles.
For so has the Lord commanded us, saying, ‘I have set you as a light for the Gentiles, that you should bring salvation to the uttermost parts of the earth.’ ”
As the Gentiles heard this, they were glad, and glorified the word of God. As many as were appointed to eternal life believed.
The Lord’s word was spread abroad throughout all the region.
But the Jews stirred up the devout and prominent women and the chief men of the city, and stirred up a persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and threw them out of their borders.
But they shook off the dust of their feet against them, and came to Iconium.
The disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.
b: In the last devotion, Paul’s sermon ended on a decision: trust this man and be justified, or be a scoffer. Once the words were spoken, what remained to be seen was how the hearers would respond.

Today is the end of chapter 13 and also the outcome of this stop at Antioch of Pisidia. The same message, in the same city, between two Sabbaths, bore two entirely opposite fruits: on one side, eagerness, gladness, spreading through the region; on the other, jealousy, slander, expulsion. And in the last verse Luke gives an unexpected closing: those driven out and the disciples who remained were “filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.”
I. “They begged that these words might be spoken to them the next Sabbath”—The First Response Was Eagerness

The response on the first Sabbath was good. As the people left the synagogue, they begged that these words be spoken to them the next Sabbath; after the meeting broke up, many Jews and “devout proselytes”—Gentiles who had formally joined Judaism—followed Paul and Barnabas.

The two spoke to them and urged them “to continue in the grace of God.” This phrase deserves notice. They did not urge the group “to work hard at keeping it well,” but “to continue in grace.” Believing is by grace, and after believing it is still by grace; it is not that grace begins and then my own effort takes over. The word “continue” means “remain in, abide.”
• Grace is not only the entrance: it begins with grace and continues with grace; after believing, don’t secretly switch back to relying on yourself.
• Abide in grace: ask once today, am I now “abiding” in grace, or have I moved back into effort?
II. “When the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy”—The Same People Changed Their Faces Within a Week

The second Sabbath, “almost the whole city was gathered together to hear the word of God.” The people of a Roman colony city had nearly all crowded into the Jewish synagogue. This should have been the dream of the Jews for hundreds of years—Gentiles coming to seek Israel’s God; yet Luke writes: “But the Jews, seeing the multitudes, were filled with jealousy.”

Note: these Jews had asked Paul the week before to speak again, and this week they “contradicted” and “blasphemed.” The word had not changed, but the people had. The reason was not that the teaching was wrong but “the multitudes”—when Gentiles flooded in, the synagogue was no longer their synagogue, and their position was threatened.

A fish in a small pond is used to being master of the pond; one day the pond connects with the sea, and it is not glad but afraid, because in the sea it is nothing. The root of jealousy is “self”—my position, my circle, my importance. The more widely the gospel spreads, the more uneasy people of self become.
• The root of jealousy is self: it is not that the word was wrong but that my position was threatened.
• Examine my unease: when others receive, when the crowd no longer surrounds me, what is the first feeling in my heart?
III. “Behold, we turn to the Gentiles”—Those Who Reject Have Judged Themselves
Facing slander, Paul and Barnabas “spoke out boldly.” This is a word often used in Acts, meaning speaking openly, fearlessly, without holding back. They said two things.

First, it was necessary that God’s word be spoken to you first—this is order, not favoritism; in every city they went first to the synagogue. Second, “seeing you thrust it from yourselves, and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life.” It was not God who judged them unworthy; they judged themselves. Those who reject the gospel are never shut out of the door; they themselves turn and walk away.

Then they quoted Isaiah: “I have set you as a light for the Gentiles, that you should bring salvation to the uttermost parts of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6). This was originally from the Servant Song about the Messiah, yet Paul said “the Lord has commanded us”—he took the Lord’s mission as his own. This is not presumption but self-denial: when a person is no longer himself within but Christ, Christ’s mission naturally becomes his mission.
• Rejection is self-judgment: no one is shut out by God; people walk away themselves.
• The Lord’s mission becomes mine: for a person emptied of self, the Lord’s heart is his heart; if the Lord wants to go to the ends of the earth, he goes.
IV. “As many as were appointed to eternal life believed”—The Glad Ones, and the Word of the Lord Spreading Everywhere

The Gentiles, hearing this, “were glad and glorified the word of God.” The same sentence: Jews heard it and were jealous; Gentiles heard it and were glad; the difference was not in the words but in the hearts. Then Luke wrote a much-discussed line: “As many as were appointed to eternal life believed.”

Luke does not explain; he simply places God’s appointing and people’s believing side by side—just as in chapter 1, when recording Judas, he set God’s prophecy beside Judas’s responsibility. God’s choosing is real, and people’s believing is real, and the two do not conflict. This line is not for making people guess whether they have been appointed but for letting those who believe know: you can believe because God first chose you—so that you cannot boast.
So “the word of the Lord was spreading throughout all the region.” What spread was the word, not Paul’s name.
• Faith is grace: that I can believe is not because I am smarter than others but because God worked first.
• What spread was the word: the focus is always on the word, not on the one who preaches.
V. “They shook off the dust of their feet… the disciples were filled with joy”—Those Driven Out Lost None of Their Joy

The Jews “stirred up the devout and prominent women and the chief men of the city”—Gentile noblewomen and officials who sympathized with Judaism and had influence in the city—and raised persecution against the two, driving them out of the region.

Paul and Barnabas “shook off the dust from their feet against them.” This was the Lord’s instruction when He sent out the disciples: if people do not receive you, shake off the dust from your feet (Luke 9:5). It means: we have preached to you, the responsibility returns to you, and we do not carry your dust with us. Then they went to Iconium, the next city, about ninety miles to the southeast.

The last verse: “The disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.” Those driven out and the new disciples who remained to face persecution were all filled with joy. This joy has nothing to do with circumstances—the circumstances were being driven out; this joy has to do with the Holy Spirit. Relying on the Spirit with the heart makes one glad; relying on the head makes one anxious.
• Shake off the dust without resentment: return the responsibility, leave the dust, and don’t carry bitterness to the next city.
• Joy has nothing to do with circumstances: being able to be full of joy though driven out is because the King in the heart has not changed.
The Light of the 321 Principles: The Focus Is on Jesus, Not on Myself, Not on Others, Not on Circumstances
This passage at the end of chapter 13 sets three kinds of focus before us.

The jealous Jews had their focus on themselves—my synagogue, my position, my importance. When the crowds grew, they were filled with jealousy. The glad Gentiles had their focus on the word—what they praised was God’s word, not Paul. The disciples who were driven out had their focus on Jesus—so though the circumstance was being driven out, their hearts were full of joy and filled with the Holy Spirit.

People of self spend their lives pulled along by three things: how I am, how others are, how circumstances are. People emptied of self are pulled by only One. Paul took “I have set you as a light for the Gentiles” as his mission because within him it was no longer he but Christ; he shook off the dust and went to Iconium because his joy lay not in how the people of the city treated him but in the Lord who sent him.

Building God’s system is exactly such a group of people: able to continue in grace, able to rejoice at others’ gain, able to be driven out without resentment, able to keep preaching in the next city. They let Jesus be King, so circumstances cannot be their king.
a: Abide in Grace
After believing, don’t secretly switch back to relying on yourself; today still continue in the grace of God.
Rejoice in Others’ Gain
When the crowd no longer surrounds me and others are blessed, practice rejoicing from the heart.
Take Up the Lord’s Mission
Wherever the Lord wants to go, I will go; His heart is my heart.
Don’t Boast
That I can believe is because God chose first; there is nothing to boast of.
Shake Off the Dust Without Resentment
When rejected or misunderstood, return the responsibility, lose no joy, and go to the next city.
q: The Jews asked Paul to come again the week before and this week were jealous and slandered, only because of “the multitudes.” Recall the last time others received and the crowd no longer surrounded you: what was the first feeling that arose? What does that feeling show about who is king in your heart?

“The disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit”—at the very time they were being driven out. Do you have a “driven out” situation right now? Does your joy follow circumstances or follow the Holy Spirit?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that with the same message, in the same city, You still caused the glad ones to believe and made Your word spread throughout the region. Thank You for letting us see that those driven out can be full of joy, because the source of joy is the Holy Spirit, not circumstances.
Lord, we confess that there is also the jealousy of those Jews in us—when the crowd no longer surrounds us and when others receive more than we do, our hearts are not glad. Forgive us, and remove the self within us that centers on position. Make us continue in Your grace, not moving back after believing to rely on our own effort; make us take Your mission as our own, so that where You want to go to the ends of the earth, we will go. And give us the freedom to shake off the dust, carrying no bitterness when rejected, going to the next city still full of joy and filled with the Holy Spirit. Be King in our hearts, and let circumstances not be our king. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: In Iconium, they entered together into the synagogue of the Jews, and so spoke that a great multitude both of Jews and of Greeks believed.
But the disbelieving Jews stirred up and embittered the souls of the Gentiles against the brothers.
Therefore they stayed there a long time, speaking boldly in the Lord, who testified to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands.
But the multitude of the city was divided. Part sided with the Jews, and part with the apostles.
When some of both the Gentiles and the Jews, with their rulers, made a violent attempt to mistreat and stone them,
they became aware of it and fled to the cities of Lycaonia, Lystra, Derbe, and the surrounding region.
There they preached the Good News.
b: In the last devotion, Paul and Barnabas were driven out of Antioch of Pisidia. They shook off the dust from their feet and went to Iconium, while the disciples who remained were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit. Those driven out did not lose heart and those who remained were not dejected; this is the scene only a church where the Holy Spirit is King can show.

From Antioch to Iconium, along the Roman highway to the southeast, is nearly ninety miles. They walked this road wounded. Yet on arriving at Iconium, the first thing they did was—enter the synagogue again.
I. “Went together into the synagogue of the Jews”—Just Driven Out, and They Went In Again
Verse 1 says that in Iconium the two “went together into the synagogue of the Jews.”

Iconium was a large city on the border of Phrygia and Lycaonia, today’s Konya in Turkey, a hub of trade routes since ancient times. It had a Jewish community and Greeks, that is, Greek-speaking Gentiles. As soon as Paul arrived, he went first to the synagogue, as always, his consistent principle: to the Jew first, and also to the Greek (Romans 1:16).

It is worth noting that they had just been driven out by the synagogue people of the last city. By ordinary human feeling, when one has been hurt by a kind of people, the next time he meets the same kind he first builds a wall inside. Paul did not. His route was decided not by wounds but by the Lord’s commission.

The same message that drew persecution in Antioch in Iconium “so spoke that a great multitude both of Jews and of Greeks believed.” The same speakers, the same content, a different result—results are never something the speaker can control.
• Don’t let wounds draw the route: having been hurt by people does not mean the Lord’s commission changes course.
• The result is not in my hands: faithfulness is mine, the harvest is the Lord’s.
II. “Stirred up the souls of the Gentiles, and made them evil affected against the brothers”—Attack Often Begins with Speech

Verse 2: “The unbelieving Jews stirred up the souls of the Gentiles.” “Stirred up” means to incite and agitate; “made evil affected” in the original is more direct: to make their souls bad, that is, to “poison.” They put poison in the Gentiles’ hearts so that they became hostile toward “the brothers.”

Note this title—“brothers.” Luke calls those newly believing “brothers,” which shows the church in Iconium had been born and Jews and Gentiles had become one family in Christ. The target of the attack was exactly this newborn family. And the method of attack was not the sword but the tongue. First make people’s hearts turn bad, and then there will naturally be those who pick up stones. Satan need not act himself; he need only plant hostility in people’s hearts, and people will act for him.

Back to ourselves: when someone speaks into my ear of a brother’s faults, is my heart immediately “poisoned,” or do I first quietly return before the Lord? People of self are most easily stirred up, because “self” always likes to hear that others are worse than oneself; a person emptied of self hears it and has no place within to receive the poison.
• Guard the ears: whether a word can get into the heart—the door is on my side.
• Guard the tongue: don’t be the one who stirs people up, and don’t be the one who passes words along.
III. “They stayed there a long time, speaking boldly in the Lord”—Persecution Came, and They Stayed Even Longer
The connecting word at the start of verse 3 carries the sense of “therefore” in the original: because some stirred up and some became hostile, “therefore” the two stayed there a long time.

This is an unreasonable reaction. By common sense, when the wind turns wrong one should pack up. They instead lengthened the itinerary and “spoke boldly in the Lord.” “Boldly” means speaking openly, frankly, without concealment; “in the Lord” shows this boldness did not come from temperament but from that Lord. The Lord also responded to them: “granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands,” bearing witness “to the word of his grace.” The miracles were not for the miracles themselves but to prove that the message concerning grace was true.

When a sailboat meets a headwind, an inexperienced sailor furls the sail and waits for the wind to turn; a veteran helmsman knows that by adjusting the angle of the sail, even a headwind can push the boat forward. Paul and Barnabas did not wait for the wind to change before preaching; they took the headwind as the power to keep moving. Persecution did not make them shut their mouths; it made them rely on the Lord all the more.
• A headwind is not a reason to stop the boat: as long as the Lord is there, the sail can stay open.
• Boldness has a source: only those who rely on the Lord can be bold; those who rely on themselves only grit their teeth.
IV. “The multitude of the city was divided”—The Gospel Does Not Create Division; It Only Reveals Hearts
Verse 4: “But the multitude of the city was divided.” “Divided” in the original is “split apart,” the root of the word “schism.”

Some think the gospel should bring everyone into harmony. But the Lord Jesus Himself said that He came not to bring peace on the earth but a sword (Matthew 10:34). When the gospel arrives, hearts are revealed: some side with the Jews, some with the apostles.

It is like lighting a lamp in a dark room. When the lamp comes on, some welcome the light gladly and some hurry to draw the curtains. The lamp did not create the darkness; the darkness was already there; the lamp only reveals each person’s attitude toward light. The gospel is the same: it does not create division, only reveals what was already in people’s hearts as two choices. So we need not be alarmed that “some oppose.” What matters is not that everyone agrees with me but that I myself stand on the side of the light.
• The dividing line is inevitable: where there is light there is shadow; no need to be alarmed by shadows.
• Which side am I on: the question is never how others choose but where I stand now.
V. “When the apostles learned of it, they fled”—Fleeing Can Also Be Obedience

Verses 5–7: the situation escalated. “When there was an attempt made both by the Gentiles and the Jews with their rulers, to treat them shamefully and to stone them.” Two groups that had looked down on each other now joined hands to oppose the gospel; even the rulers joined. Stoning was the Jewish penalty for blasphemers; this was no longer expulsion but a bid to take their lives.
“They became aware of it, and fled to the cities of Lycaonia, Lystra and Derbe, and the surrounding region.”

The word “fled” makes some people uncomfortable. Hadn’t they just stayed a long time and spoken boldly? Why flee now? This is in fact the Lord’s own teaching: “When they persecute you in this city, flee into the next” (Matthew 10:23). Staying is relying on the Lord; leaving is also relying on the Lord. The key is not staying or going but whether it is the Lord’s guidance. A person of self will stay stubbornly to prove he is brave, or leave early to protect himself; a person emptied of self asks only one thing: what does the Lord want me to do?

Verse 7 is only a short sentence: “There they preached the gospel.” The place changed; the ministry did not. The devil wanted to block one city with stones, yet God used those stones to send the gospel into two cities.
• Staying and going are both obedience: as long as it is the Lord’s guidance, there is no higher or lower.
• Change the place, not the mission: wherever one is pushed, one still does the same thing.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Rely on the Lord, Not on Circumstances

In these seven verses the circumstances kept changing: first a great crowd believed, then hearts were poisoned, then division, and finally stones. If the heart had been set on circumstances, Paul and Barnabas should have swung wildly over these days—first excited, then aggrieved, then afraid. Yet Luke describes them with a single phrase: “in the Lord.”

The focus is on Jesus, not on myself, not on others, not on circumstances. When circumstances were good, they preached; when circumstances were bad, they stayed longer and spoke more boldly; when circumstances became life-threatening, they left as guided and kept preaching in the new place. What changed was the outside; what did not change was the One relied on inside.

This is what the Holy Spirit is my guide looks like in life: not a formula for how to act in prosperity and how in adversity, but in both, first asking the Lord and then following. A person who relies on his own head is pulled along emotionally by circumstances; a person who relies on the Spirit with the heart, when circumstances change, finds the anchor in the heart has not moved.
a: Don’t Let Wounds Draw the Route
Whoever hurt me yesterday does not decide whom the Lord wants me to go to today.
Guard the Place That Receives Poison
When someone speaks into my ear of a brother’s faults, my heart first returns before the Lord.
Open the Sail in a Headwind
When opposition comes, don’t rush to shut my mouth; rely on the Lord all the more.
Don’t Be Alarmed by Shadows
Where the gospel goes there is a dividing line; I only need to stand on the side of the light.
Stay or Go, Listen to the Lord
Don’t stay stubbornly to prove bravery, and don’t leave early to protect myself.
q: Think: has some comment about a brother or sister recently quietly “poisoned” your heart? Are you willing to bring it before the Lord today and have it cleansed?
Is the environment you are in now a tailwind or a headwind? Whichever it is, are you relying on this environment or on the unchanging Lord? What visible evidence do you have?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that Paul and Barnabas walked wounded into Iconium, and there You caused a great multitude of Jews and Greeks to believe. We confess that we are often decided by yesterday’s wounds as to today’s route, by one word from someone as to the temperature of our hearts, and by the favor or adversity of circumstances as to whether we speak or go.
Lord, put our focus back on You. Teach us to guard our ears before words that stir people up and to guard our tongues before a brother’s weakness; teach us in a headwind not to furl the sail but only to adjust its angle and keep relying on You; and teach us to discern when to stay and speak boldly and when to leave as You guide. Wherever You push us, may what we do remain the same thing—preaching the word of Your grace and letting You be King. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: At Lystra a certain man sat, impotent in his feet, a cripple from his mother’s womb, who never had walked.
He was listening to Paul speaking, who, fastening eyes on him, and seeing that he had faith to be made whole,
said with a loud voice, “Stand upright on your feet!” He leaped up and walked.
When the multitude saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voice, saying in the language of Lycaonia, “The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!”
They called Barnabas “Jupiter”, and Paul “Mercury”, because he was the chief speaker.
The priest of Jupiter, whose temple was in front of their city, brought oxen and garlands to the gates, and would have made a sacrifice along with the multitudes.
But when the apostles, Barnabas and Paul, heard of it, they tore their clothes, and sprang into the multitude, crying out,

“Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men of like passions with you, and bring you good news, that you should turn from these vain things to the living God, who made the sky, the earth, the sea, and all that is in them;
who in the generations gone by allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways.
Yet he didn’t leave himself without witness, in that he did good and gave you rains from the sky and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness.”
Even saying these things, they hardly stopped the multitudes from making a sacrifice to them.
b: In the last devotion, the crowd in Iconium picked up stones, and Paul and Barnabas fled, as the Lord guided them, to Lystra and Derbe in Lycaonia, where they preached the gospel.

Lystra was about twenty miles from Iconium, a small city with no synagogue—at least Luke does not mention one. This was the first time the apostles faced a crowd with no Old Testament background at all, who worshiped only Zeus and Hermes. Here they met something harder to deal with than stones: applause.
I. “A man crippled from birth, who had never walked”—He Listened First, and Only Then Was He Seen

Verse 8 describes this man on three levels: powerless in his feet, lame from his mother’s womb, never having walked. Luke was a physician, and he wants us to know that this was no passing illness but a disability fixed from birth.

Reading this, we remember the man at the Beautiful Gate in chapter 3, “lame from his mother’s womb.” Luke deliberately sets the two stories side by side: Peter healed a Jew in Jerusalem, and Paul healed a Gentile in Lystra. The same Lord and the same power, first in the holy city and now in a Gentile town.

Verse 9 says, “He heard Paul speaking.” The original is in a continuous tense: he kept on listening. Then “Paul, fixing his eyes on him and seeing that he had faith to be made whole.” Faith comes from hearing (Romans 10:17). This man listened first, and faith grew out of his listening, and only then did Paul see it.
• Listened first, then was seen: faith does not appear out of nowhere; it grows as the word enters the heart.
• God sees the inside: the crowd saw a pair of powerless feet; Paul saw a heart of faith.
II. “Stand upright on your feet!”—What Was Spoken Aloud Was a Command
In verse 10, Paul said “with a loud voice, ‘Stand upright on your feet!’”

He gave no medical explanation first, and he did not say, “Give it a try.” He gave a command, loudly and publicly. This courage has the same source as “speaking boldly in the Lord” in the last devotion. And the man’s response was to “leap up and walk”—a man who had never walked, and his first movement was not to stand but to leap.

There is a detail here that is often overlooked: what Paul asked him to do was something he had never done and could never have done. But God’s commands always carry the power to accomplish them. The man did not first have strength and then stand; he first obeyed the command, and then the strength came.
• Obedience comes before power: it is not that I get up once I have strength; I get up, and the strength comes.
• The Lord’s word carries power: when He says “Rise,” it is not a suggestion but an accomplishment.
III. “The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!”—Applause Came Faster Than Stones

In verses 11 to 13 the scene suddenly spun out of control. The crowd shouted in their local Lycaonian language, and for a while Paul and Barnabas could not understand; only when the priest of Zeus arrived at the gates with oxen and garlands did they realize what was happening.

There is some background here. The Roman poet Ovid recorded a legend circulating in this region: Zeus and Hermes once came in human form to Phrygia, and every household refused to take them in except one old couple, who received them; the whole land was then flooded, and only that old couple was blessed. The people of Lystra remembered this lesson through the generations—when the gods come, never miss them again. So Barnabas was taken for Zeus, probably because of his calm bearing, and Paul for Hermes, because Hermes was the messenger of the gods, “since he was the chief speaker.” Even the priest was mobilized, and the oxen and garlands were the proper scale for a sacrifice.

Stones are an open attack; applause is a hidden test. When stones strike the body, a person wakes up; when applause falls on the ear, a person grows intoxicated. Iconium wanted their lives, and Lystra wanted to give them glory—and the latter was actually more dangerous.
• Recognize the test inside applause: when others lift me up is exactly when the self most easily takes the throne.
• Human enthusiasm is not God’s will: however hot the crowd’s fervor, a wrong direction is still wrong.
IV. “They tore their clothes and rushed out among the crowd”—The Moment Glory Touched Them, They Tore It Off
Verse 14 is the high point of the whole passage: “But when the apostles, Barnabas and Paul, heard of it, they tore their clothes and sprang out among the multitude, crying out…”

Tearing one’s clothes was what Jews did on hearing blasphemy, a sign of extreme horror and grief. They regarded being taken for gods as blasphemy, and their speed of reaction was to “spring out”—not a second of hesitation, not a trace of room to enjoy it.

We have to be honest: if it were me, would I let that glory rest on me for a moment first? Even if only by quietly thinking, “I really am pretty good”? Paul and Barnabas had no such moment. The first words they cried out were: “We also are men of like passions with you.” The original is “men with the same nature as you”—just as capable of weakness, of sickness, of death.

With a good window, people look at the scenery outside, not at the glass itself; when the glass draws attention to itself, there is only one reason: it is dirty. A person who serves is that pane of glass. If people see the Lord through me, the glass is clean; if people stop at me and look at me, it is time for me to wipe the glass. Letting Jesus have all the glory is just this small thing in daily life: when others praise me, I turn the glory to the Lord at once and do not grab it with my mouth; when others lift me up, I immediately return to my place—I am only a man too.
• The speed of tearing: the moment glory touches me, tear it off at once and do not let it linger.
• Return to my place: pride leaves its place to take God’s, and humility stands back in it and says, “I am only a man too.”
V. “Turn from these vain things to the living God, who made the heaven, the earth, the sea, and all that is in them”—To People Without Scripture, Begin with the Sky and the Rain

Verses 15 to 18 are the first sermon in Acts addressed to purely Gentile hearers. In the synagogue Paul spoke of Abraham and David; here he mentions neither, because his hearers had never heard of them. He began with what the crowd could see: sky, earth, sea, rain, fruitful seasons, food, and gladness.

He said that all of this is how the “living God” “left not himself without witness.” In past generations God “allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways,” yet never for a moment stopped showing kindness: giving rain, fruitful seasons, filling people with food and gladness. Even in the days when you worshiped idols, it was still He who fed you.

And the response he wanted was only one: “turn from these vain things to the living God.” “Vain things” are empty things with no substance—idols are exactly so; the oxen and garlands were offered to an emptiness.

Verse 18 ends truthfully: “With these sayings they hardly restrained the multitudes from making a sacrifice to them.” It was not that everyone believed, only that the crowd was barely held back. This sermon did not bring a great crowd to repentance, but it did one thing right: it pushed the glory off man and back onto God.
• Begin where the hearer understands: with people who have no Bible, start with the meal they eat every day and the rain that falls every year.
• Grace has been there all along: even while people were worshiping idols, the One who sent the rain was already He.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Let Jesus Have All the Glory
Stones did not bring Paul down, but applause nearly did. This passage tests one of the two core principles—letting Jesus have all the glory—in an extremely concrete scene.

For a life of self, the deepest craving is not money but to be taken for a god: to be looked up to, needed, and credited. The oxen and garlands of Lystra were exactly what the self dreams of. A life emptied of self is different: when glory lands in its hands, it pushes it back at once as if it were burning hot, because it knows that glory does not belong to it.

What Paul and Barnabas tore was not only their clothes but the faintest thought in the self of keeping some glory. When they said, “We also are men,” it was humility in its plainest form: not belittling oneself but returning to one’s place, letting God be God and man be man. When man stands back in his place, God’s glory has a way forward; when man seizes the glory, the crowd can only stop at man and never see the living God who sends rain and fruitful seasons.
a: Listen First, Then Be Seen
Faith comes from hearing; today, let the word enter my heart first.
Obedience Before Power
When the Lord says “Rise,” I rise first, and the strength comes after obedience.
Be Alert to Applause
The moment I am lifted up is exactly when the self most wants the throne.
Tear It Off at Once
The instant glory touches me, I turn it to the Lord—not kept on my lips, not kept in my heart.
Wipe the Glass Clean
Let people see the Lord through me, not stop at me and look at me.
q: Think back to the last time someone praised you or lifted you up. What was your first reaction inside? How long did that glory stay on you before you turned it to the Lord?

The people of Lystra worshiped “vain things,” not knowing that the living God was the One who sent rain and fruitful seasons. In your own life, is there anything you have always credited to luck, ability, or circumstances that was really His grace?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that in Lystra, where there was no synagogue and no Scripture, You made a man who had never walked leap up and walk; thank You that even in the days when people still worshiped idols, You kept showing kindness, giving rain from heaven and fruitful seasons. We confess that we often forget that You are the One who feeds us every day.
Lord, we may be able to endure stones, but applause often makes us stumble. Give us the sensitivity and speed of Paul and Barnabas: the moment glory touches us, to tear it off at once and spring out among the crowd to cry, “We also are men.” Remove from us that self that wants to be taken for a god, and make us a clean pane of glass, so that what people see through us is You, not us. May You receive all the glory, and may every word of praise return to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: But some Jews from Antioch and Iconium came there, and having persuaded the multitudes, they stoned Paul, and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead.
But as the disciples stood around him, he rose up, and entered into the city. On the next day he went out with Barnabas to Derbe.
When they had preached the Good News to that city, and had made many disciples, they returned to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch,
strengthening the souls of the disciples, exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that through many afflictions we must enter into God’s Kingdom.
When they had appointed elders for them in every assembly, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they had believed.
They passed through Pisidia, and came to Pamphylia.
When they had spoken the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia.
From there they sailed to Antioch, from where they had been committed to the grace of God for the work which they had fulfilled.
When they had arrived, and had gathered the assembly together, they reported all the things that God had done with them, and that he had opened a door of faith to the nations.
They stayed there with the disciples for a long time.
b: In the last devotion, the people of Lystra came with oxen and garlands to sacrifice to Paul and Barnabas, and the two tore their clothes and sprang out among the crowd, barely restraining them.

The applause had not yet faded when the stones arrived. The word “but” at the beginning of verse 19 turns the whole atmosphere over. The people who wanted to make him a god yesterday picked up stones today and beat him until they supposed he was dead. This passage begins with a pile of stones, yet ends at an open door.
I. “Having stoned Paul, they dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead”—From Garlands to Stones, Only One “But” Apart

Verse 19 says, “Some Jews from Antioch and Iconium came there.” From Antioch of Pisidia to Lystra is several days’ walk; these people were not passing through but had come in pursuit. They “persuaded the multitudes”—the “poison” mentioned in the last devotion was being used again.

The crowd in Lystra truly changed their faces. The same crowd who a few days earlier cried, “The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men,” now laid hands on Paul and dragged him out of the city. People are like that: those who lift you to heaven will not necessarily stand beside you when you fall. The enthusiasm of crowds cannot be relied on; the only One who can be relied on is the Lord.

“Supposing that he was dead”—they dragged him the way one drags a corpse. When Paul later wrote in 2 Corinthians of being “stoned once” (2 Corinthians 11:25), this was the occasion. It was a wound he still remembered many years later.
• The face of the crowd turns: today’s applause and tomorrow’s stones may come from the same hands.
• Do not set the heart on people’s reactions: one whose heart is set on the Lord will not collapse when people turn on him.
II. “But as the disciples stood around him, he rose up and entered into the city”—The Quietest Sentence, the Most Powerful
In verse 20 we read, “But as the disciples stood around him, he rose up, and entered into the city.”

Luke writes with great restraint. He does not say it was a miracle, and he does not say it was not; he says only that the disciples stood around him, and then he rose up. This “standing around” was a group of people who had believed only a few days, risking the same beating, standing beside a preacher who had been taken for dead. They could do nothing; they simply stood there. And Paul rose up in the middle of that circle.

There is a possibility: later Paul said to Timothy, “You have followed… my persecutions, sufferings—those that happened to me at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra” (2 Timothy 3:10–11). Timothy was from Lystra (Acts 16:1), and among the disciples standing around Paul that day there may well have been this young man. He saw with his own eyes a man beaten like that, and then rise up and walk into the city. That scene was cut into his life more deeply than any sermon.

“Entered into the city”—not fleeing, but walking back into the very city that had just stoned him. Only the next day did he go on to Derbe. He was not frightened away; he left when he had arranged things.
• Stand beside: sometimes the greatest help we can give a brother is simply to stand there and not leave.
• Getting up is enough: being knocked down is not the problem; whether one can rise is.
III. “They returned to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch”—Turning Back into the Cities That Struck Him

In verse 21, Derbe is the farthest stop of this journey, where they “made many disciples.” From Derbe, going east over the mountains, was Paul’s hometown Tarsus, and that road back to Antioch of Syria was the shortest and the safest.
Yet Paul chose to retrace his steps: Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch—three cities that had just driven him out, beaten him, and tried to kill him.

Why? Verse 22 gives the answer: “Strengthening the souls of the disciples, exhorting them to continue in the faith.” He could not let go of those new believers. People matter more than tasks, and relationships more than things—here that is not a slogan but a man dragging a body that had been stoned back into danger to visit a few new believers.

What he said to them was also very real: “Through many afflictions we must enter into the Kingdom of God.” He did not say, “Once you believe in the Lord, everything will go smoothly.” He stood before his own scars and said: this road must pass through hardship. The word “must” in Luke’s pen is the word for God’s will—hardship is no accident but a part of the journey.
• Turn back for people: however far the work reaches, turn back for a few people.
• Tell the truth: don’t coax people to believe with “smooth sailing”; strengthen their hearts with “we must go through hardship.”
IV. “When they had appointed elders for them in every assembly, and had prayed with fasting, they entrusted them to the Lord”—What Was Built Was a System That Does Not Rely on Self
In verse 23 we read, “When they had appointed elders for them in every assembly, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord on whom they had believed.”

“Appointed” in the original carries the sense of “stretching out the hand to designate.” These churches had been founded only a few months, and the elders were only a few months in the faith; we would most likely say, “Let’s wait until they are more mature.” But Paul handed the responsibility down, and then did two things: fasted and prayed, and entrusted them to the Lord.

This is a key lesson in building God’s system. God’s system is not Paul’s system and does not depend on Paul staying to hold it up. When he left, the church could not fall, because the church depended on the “Lord on whom they had believed,” not on him.

When a parent teaches a child to ride a bicycle, the hardest step is not running alongside holding on but letting go. If the hand always holds on, the child never learns; once the hand lets go, the child wobbles and falls, but only so does he truly learn to ride. Here Paul let go. It was not that he did not care; after fasting and prayer, he placed them in hands more reliable than his own.
• Ministry with self holds on tight: as if nothing can go on without me.
• Ministry emptied of self entrusts: having prayed, it hands people to the Lord, trusting that He watches over them better than I do.
V. “They rehearsed all the things that God had done with them”—Back to the Beginning, Giving Everything to God

Verses 24 to 28 are the journey home. Passing through Pisidia, they came to Pamphylia and “spoke the word in Perga”—on the way out they had only passed through Perga, where Mark left them (13:13); on the way back they made up for it by preaching. Then they went down to the port of Attalia and sailed back to Antioch of Syria.

Verse 26 reminds us that all of this began with the fasting and prayer in Antioch: “from where they had been committed to the grace of God for the work which they had fulfilled.” With the words “the grace of God,” Luke defines the whole journey—not their ability but God’s grace.

The report in verse 27 has the same tone: “They rehearsed all the things that God had done with them, and that he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles.” The subject is God. The door was opened by God and the works were done by God; they were only the hands “with” whom He worked. The two who came back from Galatia carried the wounds of stones on their bodies and not one word of their own merit on their lips.
Then, “They stayed there no little time with the disciples.” When the work reached a pause, they returned to the family and rested.
• Remember the beginning: all the work began with “the grace of God” and should end the same way.
• The subject of the report: when telling it, the subject is God, not me.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Life First, Then Relationships, Then Ministry
In this passage Paul made three choices, each going against the instinct of the self.

Knocked down, he rose and walked back into the city; reaching the farthest stop, he turned back into the cities that had struck him to see the disciples; the churches established, he let go and entrusted them to the Lord. Behind these three choices is one order: life first, then relationships, then ministry. His own life first stood firm, then he turned back for relationships, and last of all he handed over the ministry.

The person of self puts ministry first: completing the route, expanding the territory, leaving his own mark. The person emptied of self puts people first: for a few new believers, willing to risk stones once more; so that they truly grow up, willing to let go and not hold them up.

And the purpose of all this is not to build Paul’s ministry but to build God’s system—a people who let Jesus be King, who even after the apostle is gone still stand by the Lord on whom they have believed. When Paul left Galatia, what he took away was scars, and what he left behind was a group of churches that did not depend on him. That is exactly what building God’s system should look like.
a: Do Not Live on Applause
Those who lift me up may turn on me tomorrow; my heart rests only on the Lord.
Stand Beside the Brother
When he is knocked down, perhaps all I can do is stand there and not leave.
Turn Back for People
However far the work reaches, be willing to walk back into danger for a few people.
Let Go and Entrust
After praying, hand people to the Lord, who is more reliable than I am.
God Is the Subject
When I tell it all, remember that the door was opened by Him and I was only the hands.
q: “Through many afflictions we must enter into the Kingdom of God.” The hardship you are going through now—do you treat it as an accident or as a part of the journey? Will these two views lead you to different places?
In your hands, is there a matter or a person you have always been “holding up” and dared not let go? Paul entrusted them to the Lord after fasting and prayer—when are you willing to let go?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that in the midst of the stones at Lystra You made Paul rise and walk into the city; thank You for letting a group of new disciples stand around a servant who was taken for dead. We see that Your Kingdom is entered this way—we must go through many afflictions, yet not one step is outside Your hand.
Lord, give us a heart like Paul’s: willing to rise when knocked down, willing to turn back for people when we have gone far, willing to let go and entrust them to You when we have built. Remove from us the self that clings to ministry as if nothing could go on without me, and remove also the self that floats when praised and falls when struck. Teach us to rest our hearts on You alone, and when we tell it all, let the subject always be You. May everything You do through our hands be given to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Some men came down from Judea and taught the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised after the custom of Moses, you can’t be saved.”

Therefore when Paul and Barnabas had no small discord and discussion with them, they appointed Paul and Barnabas, and some others of them, to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and elders about this question.
They, being sent on their way by the assembly, passed through both Phoenicia and Samaria, declaring the conversion of the Gentiles. They caused great joy to all the brothers.
When they had come to Jerusalem, they were received by the assembly and the apostles and the elders, and they reported everything that God had done with them.
But some of the sect of the Pharisees who believed rose up, saying, “It is necessary to circumcise them, and to command them to keep the law of Moses.”
The apostles and the elders were gathered together to see about this matter.

When there had been much discussion, Peter rose up and said to them, “Brothers, you know that a good while ago God made a choice among you that by my mouth the nations should hear the word of the Good News and believe.
God, who knows the heart, testified about them, giving them the Holy Spirit, just like he did to us.
He made no distinction between us and them, cleansing their hearts by faith.
Now therefore why do you tempt God, that you should put a yoke on the neck of the disciples which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?
But we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus,  just as they are.”
b: In the last devotion, Paul and Barnabas returned to Antioch, reported how God had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles, and stayed with the disciples a long time.

When the door opened, problems came with it. As Gentiles poured into the church, some began to ask: are they really saved? Must they first become Jews? This question looks like a theological dispute, but it touches the very core of the gospel—how exactly is a person saved? Chapter 15 is the watershed of Acts, where the church nearly changed the gospel into something else.
I. “Unless you are circumcised after the custom of Moses, you can’t be saved”—Add a Little to the Gospel, and It Is No Longer the Gospel

In verse 1, “Some men came down from Judea.” From Jerusalem to Antioch is “down”—geographically so, and in their hearts too: from the mother church to a branch, from the orthodox center to the margin. They came to “teach the brothers,” in a tone of authority.

What they said was short: “Unless you are circumcised after the custom of Moses, you can’t be saved.” Notice that they did not deny Jesus or deny the cross; they only attached one condition behind it. Believing in Jesus, plus circumcision, and then you can be saved.

If the giver attaches a bill to a gift, however small the amount, it is no longer a gift but a transaction. The gospel is the same. If any “and you must” is added behind justification by faith, grace has gone bad. These men were not taking anything away from the gospel; they were adding something—and adding is as deadly as subtracting.

We do not argue about circumcision today, but the temptation to “add” has never left: believing in Jesus, plus a certain spiritual display, a certain length of service, a certain standard of living, and only then is one a real Christian. Each time I discount someone else’s salvation, it is mostly because I have quietly added a condition—and that condition is usually exactly the one I happen to be able to meet myself.
• Recognize the “add”: any “and you must” behind grace is a bill.
• Examine my own conditions: are the demands I place on others exactly the ones I am good at?
II. “Great dissension and discussion”—Some Things Cannot Be Given Up for the Sake of Peace
In verse 2, “Paul and Barnabas had no small discord and discussion with them.” The wording in the original is strong: no small conflict, no small debate.

Paul was not a contentious man. For his own sake he could be beaten, driven out, and stoned without hitting back; but for the truth of the gospel he would not yield an inch. Looking back on this later he said, “We didn’t give in to them, no, not for an hour, that the truth of the Good News might continue with you” (Galatians 2:5).

Here is a distinction: when it concerns the self, yield; when it concerns the Lord’s truth, do not. A person of self does exactly the opposite—fights to the end for his own face, yet compromises on truth because compromise offends fewer people.

After the debate, “they appointed Paul and Barnabas” and some others to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and elders. Paul had the authority of an apostle and could have announced the conclusion himself; yet he submitted to the church’s decision and brought the question before everyone. Truth cannot be yielded, but the way of handling truth must fit the system—this too is emptiness of self.
• Discern what to contend for: for the self, yield; for the Lord’s truth, do not.
• Submit to the system: even when right, follow the order and do not settle it alone.
III. “Declaring the conversion of the Gentiles, and they caused great joy to all the brothers”—All the Way, They Were Not Complaining

In verses 3 and 4 the church sent them on their way. From Antioch to Jerusalem by land one passes through Phoenicia and Samaria. What did they do all along the road? “Declaring the conversion of the Gentiles.”

Imagine: they were being accused of preaching an incomplete gospel and were going to a meeting on which the survival of their own ministry hung. If it were me, I would probably spend the whole road calculating how to argue, how to answer, who would stand on my side. Yet they spoke all the way of what God had done, and “caused great joy to all the brothers.”

The focus was on Jesus—not on themselves, not on others, not on the circumstances. Their focus did not fall on the few who attacked them but on God; and on arriving in Jerusalem, they “reported all the things that God had done with them”—again the same sentence, with God as the subject.
• What we speak on the road shows what is in the heart: in days of accusation, the mouth still speaks of what God has done.
• The subject of the telling: all the way it is “what God has done,” not “the wrong I suffered.”
IV. “Some of the sect of the Pharisees stood up”—One Who Has Believed May Still Carry the Old Framework

In verse 5, in Jerusalem too some stood up: “But some of the sect of the Pharisees who believed.” Luke makes a point of noting that they were believers and also Pharisees. They truly believed in Jesus, but had not put down the Pharisaic framework.

This deserves our alertness more than the attack from outside. A person can believe for many years and still interpret grace with old concepts. Their motive may have been devout—fearing that the Gentiles would not be holy enough, that the church would not be pure enough. But a devout motive can just as well lead people back under the law. Only a changed way of thinking changes a life; if the thinking has not changed, a person still measures himself and others by the old measure. In verse 6, “The apostles and the elders were gathered together to see about this matter”; the church neither avoided it nor suppressed it, but laid it open and discussed it.
• Believing does not mean the framework has been replaced: ask yourself, is the ruler I measure my brother with the ruler of grace or of law?
• Do not avoid: a disagreement in the church, laid open and discussed before the Lord, is better than one pressed down to ferment in the heart.
V. “We believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they are”—Peter’s Last Speech
In verses 7 to 11, “When there had been much discussion,” Peter stood up. This is the last time he speaks in Acts.

He offered no theory but his experience. “God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the nations should hear the word of the Gospel”—he meant the house of Cornelius, more than ten years earlier. On that day the Holy Spirit fell on Gentiles who had not been circumcised, “just like he did to us.” Peter’s argument has only one point: God has already acted first; by what right do we add conditions afterward? “God, who knows the heart,” looks at the heart, not at a mark in the flesh; “cleansing their hearts by faith”—the evidence of cleansing is faith, not circumcision.

Then he asked a very weighty question: “Why do you put a yoke on the neck of the disciples which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?” It is honest to the point of alarming: the yoke of the law we could not bear ourselves, so how could we ask others to bear it?

Verse 11 is the conclusion of the whole passage, and the clearest sentence about salvation in the whole book of Acts: “We believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they are.” Notice the order—he did not say, “They are saved just as we are,” but “we are saved just as they are.” The way Jews are saved is no different from the way Gentiles are saved; both are by grace.
• God acted first: He has already given the Holy Spirit, and people should not add conditions afterward.
