• I am just as they are: it is not that I received it first and then consider whether to share it with him; we are all saved alike by grace.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Before Grace, There Is No “Them and Us”
The most moving words in this passage are Peter’s “made no distinction between us and them.”

“Making a distinction between them and us” is the deepest habit of a life of self. The self needs a boundary so that it can stand on the right side: the circumcised and the uncircumcised, the senior and the newcomer, the well-behaved and the unruly. Once the line is drawn, the self has somewhere to stand and can feel a little higher than others.

A life emptied of self sees something else: I am just as they are, saved by grace. Once this truly enters the heart, the boundary has no place to stand. Here humility looks very concrete: when I look at a brother who has just believed and does not yet understand anything, I do not think, “He still needs to reach my level,” but “I am just as he is, depending wholly on the Lord’s grace.”

Only emptiness of self can bring unity. Whether Antioch and Jerusalem, Gentile and Jew, can become one church depends on whether each person is willing to put down “them and us” and return to this one sentence: “We believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus.”
a: Recognize the Bill
Any “and you must” behind grace is a condition I added.
Discern What to Contend For
Yield for the self, not for the truth, but handle it in a way that fits the system.
Speak of God’s Works on the Road
In days of accusation, let the mouth speak of what God has done, not of the wrong.
Replace the Old Ruler
The ruler I use to measure my brother is the ruler of grace, not of law.
I Am Just as They Are
Look at each person and remember first that I too depend wholly on the Lord’s grace.
q: Think honestly: do you have an unwritten list in your heart of what a “real Christian” is? How many items on that list are exactly ones you are able to do yourself?

Peter said, “We are saved just as they are.” Think of a brother or sister you feel is “not enough yet”—if you are just like him, depending wholly on the Lord’s grace, how would your attitude toward him differ today?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that when the church nearly changed the gospel into something else, You spoke again through Peter’s mouth: we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus. We confess that we often quietly add conditions behind grace, and those conditions are often exactly the ones we ourselves can meet.
Lord, remove from us the boundary of “them and us,” so that when we look at each brother and sister we first remember that we too are saved by grace. Teach us to discern when to yield and when not to: to put down what is for ourselves, and to give no ground for Your truth, yet still submit to the order of Your household. Replace the ruler of the law in our hands, so that we measure ourselves by Your grace and measure others by Your grace. May Your church be one through emptiness of self. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: All the multitude kept silence, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul reporting what signs and wonders God had done among the nations through them.
After they were silent, James answered, “Brothers, listen to me.
Simeon has reported how God first visited the nations to take out of them a people for his name.
This agrees with the words of the prophets. As it is written,
‘After these things I will return. I will again build the tabernacle of David, which has fallen. I will again build its ruins. I will set it up
that the rest of men may seek after the Lord; all the Gentiles who are called by my name, says the Lord, who does all these things.’
“All of God’s works are known to him from eternity.
Therefore my judgment is that we don’t trouble those from among the Gentiles who turn to God,
but that we write to them that they abstain from the pollution of idols, from sexual immorality, from what is strangled, and from blood.
For Moses from generations of old has in every city those who preach him, being read in the synagogues every Sabbath.”
b: In the last devotion, Peter stood up and brought the debate back to one sentence: “We believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they are.”

When Peter finished, the assembly fell quiet. But the council had not yet reached a conclusion. Peter spoke of experience, and however real an experience is, it needs a higher standard to confirm it. So the last one to speak was not an apostle but James; and what he brought out was not another testimony but Scripture.
I. “All the multitude kept silence”—the Debate Stopped and the Listening Began

In verse 12, “All the multitude kept silence.” Before, “there had been much discussion”; here, the whole assembly is quiet. For a meeting that had just been so heated to grow silent and listen is itself the work of the Holy Spirit.

What did they listen to? “Listened to Barnabas and Paul reporting what signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles through them.” Here Luke puts Barnabas before Paul—in Jerusalem, Barnabas was the one everybody knew and trusted better. The subject of what they reported was still God: what God had done through them.

Sometimes our problem is not that we cannot speak but that we will not stop and listen. A person of self, while another is speaking, already has his mind preparing a rebuttal; a person emptied of self can be quiet, because what he wants to hear is not who wins but what God has done.
• Be quiet first: only when the debate stops can we hear what God has done.
• Listen to what God has done: when the focus turns from “who is right” to “what God has done,” the meeting changes direction.
II. “James answered”—The One Most Qualified to Insist on the Law Let Go
In verse 13, “After they were silent, James answered.”

This James was the brother of the Lord Jesus, and by now the leader of the church in Jerusalem. He carried great weight among Jewish believers, and early church tradition called him “James the Just,” saying he kept the law strictly and prayed on his knees in the temple so often that his knees grew hard like a camel’s. In other words, if anyone in the room was most qualified to say, “The Gentiles must keep the law too,” it was he.
He opened by calling Peter “Simeon”—the old Hebrew form of the name, a Jew speaking to Jews. And this most Jewish of men, in the whole council, stood on the side of the Gentiles.

Humility is to put down power and return to one’s place. James had power, a position, and seniority, yet he let what he held to submit to the facts God had shown. This is our hardest lesson: not letting go on what we do not understand, but letting go on the very matter we understand best and are most qualified to speak about.
• Hardest to release where I know best: on the point I am most sure of, am I willing to let God have the last word?
• Position submits to fact: what God has already done is greater than my position.
III. “The words of the prophets agree with this”—Experience Must Be Read Within Scripture

In verses 14 to 18, James first sums up Peter’s testimony: God “took from among them a people for his name.” To Jewish ears this was astonishing—the word “people” had always been reserved for Israel; now God had chosen a “people” from among the Gentiles.

Then he said the most crucial sentence of the council: “This agrees with the words of the prophets.” He quoted Amos 9: God will rebuild the tent of David which has fallen, “that the rest of men may seek after the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by my name.” So the Gentiles’ turning to the Lord was not a new policy but a plan God had written down hundreds of years before; “who makes these things known from of old.”

There is an order here worth noting. Peter brought the work of the Holy Spirit, and James brought the word of Scripture—the Holy Spirit is my guide and Scripture is my standard, and when the two agree, the council has a foundation. Experience is precious, but experience cannot be its own standard; even the most real experience must be set back into Scripture, to see whether it agrees with what God has already said.

However beautiful a puzzle piece is, it must be set within the whole picture before one knows whether it is in the right place. Peter’s Cornelius and Paul’s Galatia were each a real piece; what James did was to bring out the whole picture and check—and when it matched, everyone knew this was not human opinion but the work of God.
• Experience is not its own standard: any stirring and any experience must be checked against Scripture.
• Two foundations agree: the Holy Spirit’s guidance will not conflict with Scripture’s standard; if they conflict, the mistake is surely in my understanding.
IV. “We should not trouble those from among the Gentiles who turn to God”—The Door of Grace Has No Threshold

In verse 19, “Therefore my judgment is that we don’t trouble those from among the Gentiles who turn to God.” “My judgment” in the original carries the weight of a leader; yet he did not issue an order but offered a judgment and left it to everyone.

The word “trouble” means adding difficulty and increasing burdens. James’ conclusion is the same as Peter’s: do not put a yoke on their necks. The door of salvation does not require Gentiles to become Jews first in order to enter.

What does this mean for us? In the church there is always a tendency to feel that a newcomer must first “be like us” to count as truly in—speak our language, keep our rules, look like us. James says: do not trouble them. The Lord opened the door; the threshold was not added by us.
• Add no threshold: the door the Lord opened—I will not set another checkpoint at its entrance.
• See “turning to God”: they are turning to God, not turning to us.
V. “But that we write to them that they abstain”—Consideration within Freedom

In verses 20 and 21, James proposed four things: abstain from the pollution of idols, from sexual immorality, from what is strangled, and from blood. These four are not conditions for salvation—the question of salvation had just been settled; this is a question of fellowship.

Why these four? Verse 21 gives the reason: “For Moses from generations of old has in every city those who preach him, being read in the synagogues every Sabbath.” In every city there were Jewish brothers who had heard the books of Moses from childhood, and these four matters were their deepest taboos, especially those concerning food. If the Gentile brothers had no regard for them, the two sides could not eat at the same table—and in that age, not sharing a table meant not being one family.

It is like a new member joining a household. No one asks the newcomer to become another person, but when sharing a table, a few things need mutual consideration: one does not eat spicy food, another cannot touch seafood. Consideration is not a rule; it is love. The Gentiles did not need to be circumcised, yet were willing to lay down a few freedoms for the sake of their Jewish brothers—this is emptiness of self within grace: I have freedom, but I do not use my freedom to make my brother stumble.
• Freedom is not for myself: what I have the right to do is not necessarily what I should do for my brother.
• Sharing a table matters more than holding my ground: being able to sit down and eat together matters more than proving I am right.
The Light of the 321 Principles: The Holy Spirit Guides, Scripture Confirms, Let God Have the Last Word

The conclusion of the Jerusalem Council was not reached by a vote, nor by pressing someone’s seniority. It came about this way: Peter reported what the Holy Spirit had done, Barnabas and Paul reported what God had done, and James brought out Scripture and said, “This agrees with the words of the prophets.”

This is exactly what the three foundations look like in a real meeting. The Holy Spirit is my guide—God had already acted first through the Spirit; Scripture is my standard—what God does must be confirmed by what He has said; Jesus is my example—Peter’s sentence, “We are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus,” brought everything back to Him.

And what lets the three foundations work is a group of people emptied of self. James, most entitled to insist, let go; Paul, with the most reason to argue, quietly reported; the whole assembly kept silence to hear what God had done. When no one is in a hurry to make himself win, God has room to speak. This is what letting Jesus be King looks like at the meeting table: not who won, but that the Lord won.
a: Be Quiet Before Speaking
Put down “who is right” and first listen to what God has done.
Let Go Where I Know Best
On the point I am most entitled to insist on, let God have the last word.
Check Experience Against Scripture
Set every stirring and experience back into Scripture to check it.
Set No Threshold
The door the Lord opened—I add no checkpoint at its entrance.
Lay Down Freedom for the Brother
Being able to share a table matters more than proving I am right.
q: On what matter are you most sure and most entitled to speak? If what God has done differs from your position on it, would you let go as James did?
Is there something you are “free to do” that makes it hard for a brother or sister to sit at the same table with you? For his sake, are you willing to lay it down?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that in the most crucial meeting of the church, You made the one most entitled to insist let go, made the one with the most reason to argue grow quiet, and made the whole assembly keep silence to hear what You had done. Thank You for having determined this from of old and for confirming Your work with the words of the prophets.
Lord, teach us to follow the Holy Spirit rather than lean on ourselves: let our experience submit to Your word and our position submit to Your work, especially letting go on the very matter we understand best and are surest of. Remove from us the habit of adding thresholds at the door, so that we do not trouble those You have received; and give us consideration within grace, willing to lay down a few freedoms for our brothers so that we can share a table. May You be King in every one of our deliberations, and may the conclusion always be that You won, not I. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Then it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole assembly, to choose men out of their company, and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas: Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas, chief men among the brothers.
They wrote these things by their hand: “The apostles, the elders, and the brothers, to the brothers who are of the Gentiles in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia: greetings.
Because we have heard that some who went out from us have troubled you with words, unsettling your souls, saying, ‘You must be circumcised and keep the law,’ to whom we gave no commandment;
it seemed good to us, having come to one accord, to choose out men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul,
men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
We have sent therefore Judas and Silas, who themselves will also tell you the same things by word of mouth.
For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us, to lay no greater burden on you than these necessary things:
that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from things strangled, and from sexual immorality, from which if you keep yourselves, it will be well with you. Farewell.”
So, when they were sent off, they came to Antioch. Having gathered the multitude together, they delivered the letter.
When they had read it, they rejoiced over the encouragement.
Judas and Silas, also being prophets themselves, encouraged the brothers with many words and strengthened them.
After they had spent some time there, they were sent back with greetings from the brothers to the apostles.
But Paul and Barnabas stayed in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord, with many others also.
b: In the last devotion, James brought out the words of the prophets to confirm the work of the Holy Spirit and gave his judgment: do not trouble the Gentiles who turn to God, but write to them to abstain from a few things.

With the conclusion reached, the next question was how to deliver it to Antioch. This looks like a mere administrative procedure, yet Luke spends fourteen verses on it. For a right conclusion, delivered the wrong way, can still wound; and here the church in Jerusalem shows how truth reaches people with warmth.
I. “Choose men out of their company, and send them”—Not Only a Letter, but Two Men as Well

In verse 22, “it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole assembly.” Notice the words “the whole assembly”—the conclusion was not decided behind closed doors by a few leaders but together by the whole church. Then they did something beyond what was needed: not only writing a letter, but also choosing men to send with Paul and Barnabas.

Those chosen were “Judas who was called Barsabbas, and Silas, chief men among the brothers.” They were men of weight in the Jerusalem church, not just two runners sent casually. We will often see the name Silas later—he became Paul’s companion on the second journey.

Why was a letter not enough, but men were needed too? Verse 27 says: “They themselves will also tell you the same things by word of mouth.” A letter can convey content but not tone, expression, or warmth. The brothers in Antioch had been troubled and were hurt in heart; Jerusalem wanted them not only to know the conclusion but to feel: we are one family, and we have come ourselves.

A letter sent from distant family and the family coming to your door to say again what is in the letter are two entirely different things. People matter more than tasks, and relationships more than things—here it looks like this: the conclusion written in a letter, the relationship delivered by people.
• Beyond the message, send people: right words, spoken in person, are better than conveyed from a distance.
• Send the best: mending a relationship deserves the most weighty people in the church.
II. “To whom we gave no commandment”—Cut Off the Error, Affirm the Brothers

Verses 23 to 26 are the first half of the letter. It opens by addressing the Gentile believers in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia as “brothers”—the title itself is the answer: you are brothers, not second-class believers.

Then two actions follow. First, to cut off: “Since we have heard that some who went out from us have troubled you with words, unsettling your souls… to whom we gave no commandment.” The Jerusalem church admitted that those men had “gone out from us” and did not shift the blame; yet it stated clearly that their words did not represent the church. “Troubled” means made uneasy, and “unsettling” in the original means to dismantle or overturn—very strong words; the church did not spare the error.

Second, to affirm: “our beloved Barnabas and Paul,” “men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.” The very authority of Paul and Barnabas had just been attacked by those men; now the Jerusalem church publicly called them “beloved” in a letter and mentioned that they had risked their lives—the stones of Lystra were known in Jerusalem.

Both of these can only be done by a church emptied of self. To admit that an error went out from ourselves requires putting down face; to affirm others’ labor publicly requires putting down comparison.
• Admit and do not shift the blame: if the error went out from me, say “from us.”
• Affirm the brothers in public: do not hold back from saying “beloved” before everyone and naming what he has given.
III. “It seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us”—The Conclusion Was Heard, Not Forced
Verses 28 and 29 are the core of the letter and the most astonishing sentence of the whole chapter: “For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us…”

“The Holy Spirit and us”—they put the Holy Spirit before themselves and said this was reached together. This is no formula. Look back over the council: Peter reported how the Holy Spirit had fallen on the Gentiles, James confirmed it with Scripture, and everyone listened in silence. The conclusion surfaced under the Spirit’s guidance, Scripture’s confirmation, and everyone’s emptiness of self, so they dared to say: it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us.

And what they determined was “to lay no greater burden on you than these necessary things.” The Lord Jesus used the word “burden” of the Pharisees, who “tie up heavy burdens, hard to carry, and lay them on men’s shoulders” (Matthew 23:4). The church refused to be that kind of people. The four things to abstain from are consideration so that we can share a table; the letter ends, “If you keep yourselves from these, it will be well with you,” in a tone of exhortation, not threat.
• Ask the Spirit first: before a matter is settled, have I truly asked Him, or only asked myself?
• Lay no burden: do not bind up the standard I can meet into a burden and lay it on others’ shoulders.
IV. “They rejoiced for the encouragement”—A Letter That Bound Up the Wound
In verses 30 to 34, back in Antioch, Judas and Silas “gathered the multitude together and delivered the letter. When they had read it, they rejoiced for the encouragement.”

The word “encouragement” is the word for exhortation and shares its root with “Comforter”—calling a person to one’s side to comfort and encourage. For the Gentile brothers in Antioch this letter was an assurance: you are not second-class, you need not become Jews first to be saved, and the mother church has sent men in person to say so.

And Judas and Silas did not hand over the letter and leave. Verse 32: “Judas and Silas, also being prophets themselves, encouraged the brothers with many words and strengthened them.” They stayed for some time and, with words, strengthened those troubled hearts one by one. Then, “they were let go in peace from the brothers to those who had sent them out”—when they came, Antioch had no peace in its heart; when they left, they were sent off in peace.
A dispute that might have torn the church apart ended in this way, in “joy” and “peace.”
• Comfort must reach people: do not only announce the conclusion; stay, and strengthen people with many words.
• Peace can be seen: whether a matter was handled rightly can be seen in each other’s faces at the farewell.
V. “But Paul and Barnabas stayed in Antioch”—After the Storm, Back to the Ordinary
Verse 35 says, “But Paul and Barnabas stayed in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord, with many others also.”

When the storm passed, the two apostles did not set out at once for something bigger. They stayed and did the most ordinary thing: teaching and preaching the word of the Lord. And not the two alone, but “with many others also.” The church in Antioch had already grown many who could teach, and Paul and Barnabas were only part of them.

This is what a healthy system of God looks like: not held up by a few stars but with many working together; not forever handling crisis but, after the crisis, returning to the solid ordinary—teaching, preaching, strengthening one another.
• Return to the ordinary: after a storm, the best recovery is to go back to the most ordinary ministry.
• Work together: not I alone carrying it, but “with many others also.”
The Light of the 321 Principles: Deliver the Right Conclusion with Love

The conclusion of the Jerusalem Council was right, yet Luke spends fourteen verses on “how it was delivered.” For God’s system cares not only whether the conclusion is right but also whether people were treated well.

“It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us”—this sentence is the key to the passage. A community that lets Jesus be King decides things differently from the world: not by whose voice is loudest or whose seniority is deepest, but by everyone growing quiet, hearing what the Holy Spirit says, confirming it by Scripture, and then determining together. A conclusion reached this way dares to say it was determined by the Holy Spirit and us together.

And after the conclusion was reached, the church emptied of self did three things: admitted that the error went out from its own number, publicly affirmed the brothers who had been attacked, and sent the most weighty men to speak words of comfort in person. A church of self is satisfied to win the argument; a church emptied of self, after winning the argument, still wants to keep the people. Life first, then relationships, then ministry—what Antioch finally received was not only a letter but “joy” and “peace.”
a: Go and Say It in Person
Right words are not only sent by message; be willing to go and say them face to face.
Admit, Don’t Shift Blame
If an error went out from me, admit it went out from me.
Affirm in Public
Do not hold back from naming a brother’s sacrifice and calling him “beloved” before everyone.
Ask the Spirit First
Before settling a matter, truly ask Him, not only myself.
Lay No Burden
Do not bind the standard I can meet into a load for others’ shoulders.
q: Think of a relationship you recently handled “by message”—is there a sentence that should really be spoken by going to that person in person?
“It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us.” Think of your most recent important decision: did you ask the Holy Spirit first, or ask yourself first and then ask the Spirit to stamp it?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that You gave not only the right conclusion but also taught Your church how to bring the conclusion to people with warmth. Thank You for letting us see the words “it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us”—that a people emptied of self, growing quiet to listen to You, can together determine Your heart.
Lord, we often win the argument and lose the brother; we often announce the conclusion without staying to strengthen people. Give us a heart like the Jerusalem church: willing to admit that an error went out from us, willing to affirm publicly the brothers who were attacked, willing to send the best to speak comforting words in person. Remove from us the habit of laying burdens on people’s shoulders, and the laziness that wants to dismiss a relationship with a letter. May every decision of ours be one the Holy Spirit and we determine together; may every farewell of ours be in peace. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: After some days Paul said to Barnabas, “Let’s return now and visit our brothers in every city in which we proclaimed the word of the Lord, to see how they are doing.”
Barnabas planned to take John, who was called Mark, with them also.
But Paul didn’t think that it was a good idea to take with them someone who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia, and didn’t go with them to do the work.
Then the contention grew so sharp that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus,
but Paul chose Silas and went out, being commended by the brothers to the grace of God.
He went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the assemblies.
b: In the last devotion, the letter from Jerusalem reached Antioch, and everyone rejoiced for its encouragement; Paul and Barnabas stayed in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord with many others.

A dispute that might have torn the church apart ended in joy and peace. But Luke does not let us stop there. Right away he records another dispute—this time not between Gentiles and Jews but between Paul and Barnabas, two men who had been stoned together and risked their lives together for the Lord. Scripture does not cover for them, and that is exactly why it can be trusted.
I. “Let’s return now and visit our brothers… and see how they are doing”—What Was in Paul’s Heart Was People
Verse 36: “After some days Paul said to Barnabas, ‘Let’s return now and visit our brothers in every city in which we proclaimed the word of the Lord, and see how they are doing.’”

The motive for the second journey was not to open new ground but to “visit.” Paul’s heart was weighed down with those churches in Galatia: the disciples in Lystra, the brothers in Iconium, those filled with the Holy Spirit in Antioch of Pisidia. How were they now? “How they are doing” is a very homely phrase, like someone far from home thinking of family.

This reminds us that the core of ministry has always been people. Only in the last devotion Paul was “teaching… with many others”; the ministry in Antioch did not lack him. Yet he could not let go of those brothers far away. Life first, then relationships, then ministry—the second journey began with relationships.
• Who is on my heart: when I pray, what rises up is a group of names, or a list of tasks?
• Visiting is ministry: going back to see how the brothers are is itself the Lord’s work.
II. “Barnabas planned to take John, who was called Mark, with them”—All His Life He Gave People a Second Chance
Verse 37: “Barnabas planned to take with them John also, who was called Mark.” “Planned” in the original means “determined”—not a weak word; Barnabas had made up his mind.

This was entirely Barnabas’ style. His name means “son of encouragement” (4:36). When Saul had just believed and the disciples in Jerusalem were afraid of him, it was Barnabas who received him and brought him to the apostles (9:27); when the church in Antioch arose, it was Barnabas who went to Tarsus himself to look for Saul (11:25). Without Barnabas, there might have been no Paul as we know him.

Now the one he wanted to take was Mark—his cousin (Colossians 4:10). Mark had left the team partway through the first journey, and Barnabas of course knew it; but what he saw was not Mark’s failure but Mark’s potential. He had once given Paul a chance, and now he would give Mark one.
• See people’s potential: a person who has failed is not forever what he was.
• I was once trusted: think of who received me when I was least promising—I should receive others the same way.
III. “But Paul didn’t think it appropriate to take with them someone who had withdrawn”—He Looked at the Work, and He Had His Reasons
Verse 38: “But Paul didn’t think it appropriate to take with them someone who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia, and didn’t go with them to the work.”

Paul’s reason also stands. On the first journey, Mark left at Perga in Pamphylia (13:13), departing before the hardest mountain road. What lay ahead were the stones of Iconium and the near-death in Lystra; to take on the road someone who had once withdrawn halfway, and what if he did it again—what would become of the team? Paul looked at the “work”—“didn’t go with them to the work” was his emphasis.

So this dispute was not one right and one wrong. Barnabas was thinking of what Mark needed; Paul was thinking of what the work needed. Both loved the Lord and both had reasons, which is exactly why it was hard to reconcile.

Our disputes are mostly like this, too: not good against evil, but two views, each with reasons, in conflict. And the easiest place to go wrong is that once I feel I am right, I no longer need to hear the other.
• Being right is not being wholly right: I have a reason and the other has one too; put together, the two reasons are complete.
• Look at the work, and also at the person: the work’s needs are real, and the person’s needs are real.
IV. “They separated from each other”—Scripture Honestly Records This Scar

Verse 39: “There arose a sharp contention, so that they separated from each other.” The word “contention” in the original is very strong—“sharp conflict,” the root from which the English word “paroxysm” comes. Two co-workers quarreled until they parted.

Luke does not comment on who was right or wrong, only records the facts: Barnabas took Mark and sailed to Cyprus—Barnabas’ homeland and the starting point of the first journey; Paul chose Silas and went north by land. From this verse on, Barnabas disappears from Acts.

Some say that with the split, one team became two and the gospel spread farther. God can indeed use human weakness, and a river divided into two channels waters two fields; but the stone at the fork remains there. Luke does not write this parting as a good thing, and we need not paint it with glory.

Yet Scripture also records what came later. Years afterward Paul wrote, “Take Mark, and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service” (2 Timothy 4:11). Mark later wrote a Gospel, and Peter called him “Mark, my son” (1 Peter 5:13). Barnabas’ insistence that time was proved right, and Paul later acknowledged it.

This is the most comforting part: parting is not the end. If a person, after parting, still lets Jesus be King, the scar will heal. A person of self keeps proving himself right after parting; a person emptied of self leaves a door open, ready to admit that the other saw more than he did.
• Do not glorify a split: parting is parting, and there is no need to find a spiritual reason for it.
• Leave a door open: even when parted, do not close the matter with a final word, but leave room for the Lord to restore.
V. “Being commended by the brothers to the grace of God”—Parted, Yet Still in Grace
Verses 40 and 41: “Paul chose Silas and went out, being commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord. He went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the assemblies.”

Silas was the chief man from Jerusalem who had carried the letter to Antioch in the last devotion, a prophet, and also a Roman citizen (16:37)—the companion Paul chose for the second journey was one the Jerusalem church trusted.

And the brothers in Antioch “commended him to the grace of the Lord.” These are the same words used when the first journey set out (14:26). The church did not split into two camps because of the two apostles’ quarrel; they commended Paul to the Lord’s grace and sent him on his way. And the first thing Paul did was still “strengthening the assemblies”—back to the heart he began with.
They parted, but grace did not part. I may disagree with a brother, even part from him for a time, yet he and I are both still in the grace of the same Lord.
• Commend to the Lord’s grace: after a dispute, commend myself and the other into the Lord’s grace.
• Return to the beginning: however the road divides, the thing done is still the same—strengthening the churches.
The Light of the 321 Principles: People Matter More Than Tasks, and Grace More Than Being Right

Chapter 15 begins with a dispute over truth and ends with a dispute between co-workers. In the first, Paul did not yield an inch, because it concerned the truth of the gospel; in the second, Paul and Barnabas each held their own view, but what was at stake was a judgment about a person and a piece of work. Truth cannot be yielded, but judgments can be listened to—this is the distinction we must learn.

Barnabas saw the person, and Paul saw the work. People matter more than tasks—this sentence has no simple answer here, because in Paul’s “work” there were people too: the brothers in Galatia needed a team that would not fall apart halfway. Yet years later Paul himself said: Mark is useful to me. Time proved that the one who looked at the person saw farther.

Only emptiness of self can bring unity. This time they did not manage it, and Scripture honestly wrote it down so that we might see ourselves in our own disputes: when I am right, can I still hear the other? After parting, am I busy proving myself right, or do I leave a door open for the Lord to restore? What letting Jesus be King looks like in a dispute is simple: hand right and wrong to Him, and keep people in grace.
a: Keep People on My Heart
What rises up when I pray is a group of names, not only a list of tasks.
Give a Second Chance
Someone received me when I was least promising, and I receive others the same way.
Hear the Other’s Reason
When I am right is exactly when I most need to hear the other.
Don’t Glorify the Split
Parting is parting, but leave a door open for the Lord to restore.
Commend to the Lord’s Grace
After a dispute, commend myself and the other into the grace of the same Lord.
q: Is there a “Mark” in your life—someone who once let you down and whom you still refuse to give another chance? How would Barnabas see him?

Think of your most recent disagreement with a brother or sister. After parting, were you proving yourself right, or did you leave a door open? Are you willing today to do one thing that commends him “to the grace of the Lord”?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that You did not cover for Your servants. The dispute between Paul and Barnabas You honestly wrote in Scripture, so that we might see ourselves in our own disputes. Thank You also for letting us see the story that followed: Mark became useful to Paul, the scar of parting healed, and grace did not part.
Lord, we confess that we most easily close our ears when we are right and, after parting, busy ourselves proving we were right. Give us the eyes of Barnabas, to see people’s potential and not only their failures; and give us the humility Paul came to, willing to admit that others saw more than we did. Be King in every one of our disputes, so that we hand right and wrong to You and keep people in grace; and even if we part for a time, do not let us close the matter with a final word, so that You have room to restore. May every road we walk have us doing the same thing—strengthening Your church. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: He came to Derbe and Lystra: and behold, a certain disciple was there, named Timothy, the son of a Jewess who believed; but his father was a Greek.
The brothers who were at Lystra and Iconium gave a good testimony about him.
Paul wanted to have him go out with him, and he took and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those parts; for they all knew that his father was a Greek.
As they went on their way through the cities, they delivered the decrees to them to keep which had been ordained by the apostles and elders who were at Jerusalem.
So the assemblies were strengthened in the faith, and increased in number daily.
b: In the last devotion, Paul and Barnabas parted. Barnabas took Mark to Cyprus, and Paul chose Silas, was commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord, and went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the assemblies.

One team became two, and one of them was short a man. What Luke tells us next is exactly how God filled the gap—filled it with the one Paul would later call “my beloved child.” Paul lost Mark, and God gave him Timothy.
I. “He came to Derbe and Lystra”—Back to the Place Where He Was Stoned

Verse 1: “He came to Derbe and Lystra.” These two names were not strange to Paul. On the first journey he was stoned in Lystra and dragged out of the city, and the crowd supposed he was dead (14:19). He rose from the pile of stones and went the next day to Derbe; later he turned back into Lystra and told the disciples, “Through many afflictions we must enter into the Kingdom of God” (14:22).

Now he crossed the Taurus mountains from Cilicia and went in the opposite direction: first to Derbe, then to Lystra. The mountain passes were narrow and bandits roamed them; yet Paul went, because there were brothers there on his heart. To return to a place where one was stoned takes not only courage but a love for people greater than concern for oneself. A person of self remembers the wound and avoids that city; a person emptied of self remembers the people and walks that road again.
• Wound and brothers: do I remember a certain place because of the wound there, or because of the people there?
II. “A certain disciple was there, named Timothy”—A Young Man Raised in a Mixed Household

The name Timothy means “one who honors God.” His mother Eunice and his grandmother Lois both believed (2 Timothy 1:5); Paul says he knew the holy writings “from infancy” (2 Timothy 3:15), thanks to those two women. But his father was a Greek, that is, a Gentile, and Luke touches the tension in this household lightly with the word “but.” The text mentions only his mother as a believer, and records nothing of the kind about his father—Timothy grew up in a household divided in faith.

He probably believed when Paul first came to Lystra. Paul later reminded him: “my persecutions and sufferings—those that happened to me at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra. I endured those persecutions” (2 Timothy 3:11)—for a young person to see the man who had preached the gospel to him struck down by stones, then rise and go back into the city, is a picture that stays in the heart for a lifetime.
Timothy was half Gentile, had an unbelieving father, and was by temperament inclined to timidity (2 Timothy 1:7). Yet from just such a household God prepared the one to take up the baton from Paul.
• Environment is not qualification: an incomplete family and an impure background cannot block God’s choosing.
• Mother and grandmother: two women teaching Scripture at home raised up a co-worker of the apostle. What am I planting at home today?
III. “The brothers spoke well of him”—His Reputation Came from Two Cities

Verse 2: “The brothers who were at Lystra and Iconium gave a good testimony about him.” The two cities are about twenty miles apart. That brothers even in the neighboring city spoke well of him shows that his faith was not kept behind closed doors but had been seen and tested among the churches. “Gave a good testimony” in the original is “bore witness.” When Paul chose co-workers, the first thing he looked at was not gifts and not learning but the testimony others gave of him.

Paul later wrote to him, “Let no man despise your youth” (1 Timothy 4:12). Whether one is young is finally decided not by age but by life. There is an order here: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Timothy first had a good life among the brothers, the brothers therefore had a good relationship with him, and only then did Paul bring him onto the road of ministry. If the order is reversed, pushing someone into ministry and then trying to supply the life afterward, it often cannot be made up.
• Testimony at home: a good name among those who know me best is more real than a name outside.
• Tested first: do not rush onto the road; first let the brothers see you where you are.
IV. “Took and circumcised him”—No Giving Way on Truth, Room to Give on Method

Verse 3 is startling at first reading. In chapter 15 Paul had just fought to the end for “no need to be circumcised”; he also said that even Titus, a Greek, “was not compelled to be circumcised” (Galatians 2:3). How is it that on reaching Lystra he circumcised Timothy?

The key is “for they all knew that his father was a Greek.” By the Jewish reckoning, if the mother is a Jew, the son is a Jew; Timothy, a Jew who was not circumcised, was in Jewish eyes one who had abandoned the law. Paul entered the synagogue first in every city; to bring such a man with him would shut the synagogue door before it was even opened. Titus was a Gentile, and to circumcise him would be to say “Gentiles must be circumcised to be saved”—that is a question of truth, and no ground is given; Timothy was a Jew, and circumcising him had nothing to do with salvation but only removed an obstacle—that is a question of method, and room can be given. Paul himself said, “To the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might gain Jews” (1 Corinthians 9:20). Truth is the standard, and not one word of it may be changed; method is a bridge, and for the sake of people it can be taken down and rebuilt.

It is like visiting someone’s home and taking off your shoes at the door. Taking off your shoes does not change who you are or what you will say; it only respects the house’s custom so that people will be willing to hear you.

Nor should we forget Timothy’s side. For an adult, circumcision is painful and humiliating. He did not argue; he submitted. To lay down the comfort of his own body so that more people would hear the gospel—this is what self-denial looks like in a young man: for Jesus and for others, not for himself.
• Distinguish truth from method: on truth, no giving way; on method, for the sake of people, room to give.
• Willing to take off my shoes: for the sake of people being willing to hear the gospel, what habits and comforts of mine am I willing to lay down?
V. “Delivered the decrees to them to keep”—Faith Strengthened, Numbers Increased

Verses 4 and 5: as they went through the cities, they delivered to the disciples the decrees that the apostles and elders in Jerusalem had decided on, to keep. The “decrees” were the decision of the Jerusalem Council: Gentile believers need not be circumcised, only abstain from things offered to idols, blood, strangled animals, and sexual immorality. This letter was a release for Gentile believers—their standing as saved was formally acknowledged; for Jewish believers it was a boundary—they must no longer trouble brothers with circumcision.

The result was two things: “So the assemblies were strengthened in the faith” and “increased in number daily.” These are two indicators of a healthy church, one inward and one outward. Strong faith without growth in numbers is closed; growth in numbers without strong faith is hollow. When the truth was settled clearly, the church grew in depth and in breadth at once.

What strengthened the church was not a new ministry program but a letter that had settled the dispute. Scripture is my standard—make the truth clear, and the church is naturally strengthened; if a church stays weak, perhaps it is not lacking activities but has a blurred standard.
• Two indicators: is my life, and the group I am in, growing deep and also growing wide?
The Light of the 321 Principles: Truth Is the Standard, People Are the Focus, Method Is the Bridge

In these five verses Paul made two movements that seem contradictory: he insisted on delivering the decrees for the disciples to keep—no giving way on truth; yet he circumcised Timothy—room to give on method. And all of it was so that people might be able to hear the gospel.

Scripture is my standard, and the standard exists for people. One who takes method for truth will use circumcision to trouble brothers; one who takes truth for method will change the gospel to please people. Paul’s discernment is the discernment of one who lets Jesus be King: because his focus is on Jesus, not on his own position, he knows what cannot be given up and what, for the sake of people, can be.

Timothy’s side lets us see what emptiness of self looks like in a young man: not contending for his own rights, willing to suffer pain once for the gospel. Later Paul said, “For I have no one else like-minded, who will truly care about your state” (Philippians 2:20)—that like-minded one was the young man who obeyed in Lystra that day. Only a person emptied of self can be like-minded, and only such a person can be brought into God’s greater work.
a: Walk That Road Again
Remember a place because of its people, not because of the wound.
Plant Scripture at Home
Like Eunice and Lois, teaching a child to know Scripture at home is soil God chooses.
Have Testimony at Home First
A good name among those who know me best is more real than one outside.
Distinguish Truth from Method
On truth, no giving way; on method, for the sake of people, take off my shoes.
Submit to One Pain
Like Timothy, willing to lay down my own comfort and rights for the gospel.
q: Paul went back to Lystra, where he had been stoned, and there gained Timothy. Is there a place or relationship you do not want to return to because you were hurt there? If the Lord asked you to walk that road again, how would you respond?

Timothy submitted to circumcision for the gospel, laying down his own comfort and rights. Is there a “taking off the shoes” matter in your life—a habit or insistence you could lay down so that people would be willing to hear the gospel?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that when Paul lost Mark, You gave him Timothy; Your work has never stopped because of a gap in people. Thank You for preparing, from a household divided in faith and from a timid young man, the one to take up the baton from Your servant, so that we know circumstances are no obstacle to Your choosing.
Lord, give us Paul’s discernment, to know what is Your truth, where not one step may be given, and what is only method, which for the sake of people can be laid down. Give us also Timothy’s submission, willing to suffer once for the gospel and not to contend for our own rights. Let us plant Your word at home and first have a good testimony among the brothers, and then be brought by You into greater work. May Your church be strengthened in the faith and increase in number daily, and may You be King in it and receive all the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: When they had gone through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia.
When they had come opposite Mysia, they tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit didn’t allow them.
Passing by Mysia, they came down to Troas.
A vision appeared to Paul in the night. There was a man of Macedonia standing, begging him, and saying, “Come over into Macedonia and help us.”
When he had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go out to Macedonia, concluding that the Lord had called us to preach the Good News to them.
b: In the last devotion, Paul gained Timothy in Lystra and went through the cities of Galatia with the decrees from Jerusalem, and the churches were strengthened in the faith and increased in number daily.

Everything was going smoothly. The team was complete, the churches were steady, and all that remained was to move forward according to plan. But just then a team sent out by the Holy Spirit was stopped by the Holy Spirit twice in a row. This passage has no sermon and no church planted—only a group of people walking several hundred miles over the mountain roads of Asia Minor, not knowing where they were going.
I. “Having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia”—The One Who Closed the Door Was the Same Holy Spirit

Verse 6: “They went through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia.” “Asia” here is not today’s Asia but a Roman province whose capital was Ephesus—one of the most prosperous cities of the time. Having strengthened the churches of Galatia, Paul would naturally head west along the main road, and Ephesus was the most natural next stop.
Yet the Holy Spirit forbade it. Luke does not say how—perhaps a prophetic word, perhaps an inner restraint, perhaps closed circumstances. He says only: the Holy Spirit did not allow it.

Notice that the one closing the door here was not Satan and not persecution but the Holy Spirit. We are used to attributing obstacles to the enemy and smooth roads to God; yet this verse reminds us that sometimes the one who stops us is the very One who sent us out. Ephesus later became the city where Paul stayed longest (19:10); the work there was not canceled, only its time had not yet come.
• A good place is not necessarily the right place: however good Ephesus is, if the Holy Spirit does not allow it, don’t go.
II. “The Spirit of Jesus didn’t allow them”—Stopped a Second Time
Verse 7: “When they had come opposite Mysia, they tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus didn’t allow them.”

West was not allowed, so they turned north. Bithynia was on the south shore of the Black Sea, also a populous province, and the believers there were later among those to whom Peter wrote (1 Peter 1:1). It was a reasonable choice, yet the Spirit again did not allow it. The title “the Spirit of Jesus” appears only here in the whole Bible, as if to make us see that the One stopping Paul was the very Lord who had called him on the Damascus road.

Between the two stops lay several hundred miles of mountain road. They walked on, being shut out as they went, with no explanation at all. It is like driving by a navigation system: when the road ahead is closed, the system does not tell you why but says only, “Recalculating route”; you can only keep driving, and only on arriving at the destination do you understand what that detour meant.

Following the Holy Spirit with the heart rather than leaning on oneself with the head takes a very concrete shape here. The one who relies on his head, stopped twice, begins to analyze: did I do something wrong? Should I not have come out at all? The one who follows with the heart, stopped twice, keeps on walking, because he knows who is leading.
• A “no” is also guidance: the Holy Spirit’s “no” and His “go” come from the same Lord.
• The road without explanation: when I am stopped with no explanation, do I keep following, or stop to analyze?
III. “Passing by Mysia, came down to Troas”—Reaching the Sea, the Road Ran Out
Verse 8: “Passing by Mysia, they came down to Troas.”

Troas was a port on the Aegean Sea, near the site of ancient Troy. West not allowed, north not allowed, they could only keep going northwest until the land ended, with the sea before them. From a human point of view, this was a team with nowhere left to go: sent out with a mission, yet blocked by God at the seashore.

But it was at Troas that something happened that Luke does not state outright but hides in a word. In verse 10 the narrative person suddenly changes from “they” to “we”—Luke himself joined the team. It was very likely at Troas that Luke met Paul; this “beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14) traveled with Paul from then on and became the writer of this book.

So the detour was not in vain. God had blocked Paul at the seashore in order to give him, by the sea, a co-worker and a vision. When a person of self has nowhere to go, he sees only his predicament; when a person emptied of self has nowhere to go, he lifts his head to see what God has prepared there.
• The end is often the beginning: when we reach the end of the road, it is often just where God opens a new one.
• A gift in the detour: on this stretch of seemingly wasted road, God gave Paul a co-worker for life.
IV. “Come over into Macedonia and help us!”—The Vision Came Only at the End of the Road
Verse 9: “A vision appeared to Paul in the night. There was a man of Macedonia standing, begging him, and saying, ‘Come over into Macedonia and help us.’”

Macedonia lay across the Aegean, in Europe. This one vision was the turning point at which the gospel crossed from Asia into Europe; Philippi, Thessalonica, Corinth, and Athens all lay along this road. But Paul had no idea beforehand; in his mind were Asia and Bithynia. God’s plan is far greater than man’s plan, so man’s plan must first be blocked.

What that Macedonian said was “help us.” Not “come and preach to us” but “come and help.” In God’s eyes the gospel is the deepest help to people; the vision turned Paul’s eyes from “where shall I go” to “who is in need”—the focus moved from his own plan to people’s need.

And this vision came only after the two stops. Had Paul entered Asia smoothly at the start, he might never have walked to Troas in his whole life. God first closes a door, then opens a door; first brings a person to the end, then lets him see the direction.
• Visions are for those who have come to the end: those who refuse to keep walking never reach the place where visions are seen.
V. “Immediately we sought to go out to Macedonia”—Discerning Together, Obeying at Once
Verse 10: “When he had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go out to Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the Good News to them.”

This verse has three details. First, “we”—the vision was seen by Paul alone, but the discernment was done by the whole team. “Concluding” in the original means “putting various things together to reach a conclusion”: two stops, arriving at the sea, a vision in the night—several things set side by side, and the whole team together saw that this was God’s call. The Holy Spirit’s guidance is not one person’s arbitrary decision but something the brothers confirm together.

Second, “immediately”—they did not wait any longer or say, “Let us pray and see.” Once the direction was clear, they set out at once. The patience of the several hundred miles before was for the swiftness of this moment.

Third, “God had called us”—not “Paul decided,” not “we feel,” but “God called.” What letting Jesus have all the glory looks like here is simple: when the direction is right, I do not say that I saw it, I say that God called.
• Discern together: however clear the vision, the brothers confirm it together; it is not one person’s say.
• Move when it is clear: willing to wait while waiting, willing to move when it is clear—both are obedience.
The Light of the 321 Principles: The Holy Spirit Is My Guide, and Both Closing and Opening Are His
In these five verses the Holy Spirit did three things: forbade, did not allow, and called. The first two close doors, and the third opens one. We like the third, yet often doubt God in the first two.

The Holy Spirit is my guide—if this holds only when things go smoothly, it is not guidance but mere endorsement. True guidance includes “no.” For the old self, the life of self, what is hardest to bear is being stopped without explanation, for it means my plan and my judgment do not count. And this is exactly the training of self-denial: willing to let God’s “no” cancel my “I want,” and without needing Him to explain first.

Paul’s team shows us what a self-denied person being guided looks like: stopped, change the road; arriving at the sea, wait; seeing a vision, discern together; when it is clear, move at once. From beginning to end they did not for a moment cling to their own plan, and because of that the gospel entered Europe. If a person always wants God to follow his plan, all God can give him is as much as he planned; if a person is willing to be stopped, God can take him to places he never thought of.
a: Recognize Who Closes the Door
Not every obstacle is the enemy; sometimes the Holy Spirit is saying, “Not now.”
Keep Walking When Stopped
When there is no explanation, don’t stop to analyze; keep following.
Look Up at What Is Prepared at the Shore
At the end of the road, see what people and what words God has prepared here.
Turn from Plan to Need
Before asking “where shall I go,” ask “who needs help.”
Discern Together, Obey at Once
Have the brothers confirm the vision together, and once confirmed, do not delay.
q: Think of the most recent time you were stopped—a closed door, an unanswered prayer. Did you attribute it to the enemy, or consider that it might be the Holy Spirit saying, “Not now”? After that door closed, what did God open?

Paul’s team “discerned together and obeyed at once.” When you seek God’s guidance, is there a brother or sister who can confirm it with you? When the direction is clear, do you usually set out at once, or keep delaying?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that Your guidance is not only opening doors but also closing them. Thank You for letting us see that Paul was stopped twice, walked several hundred miles with no explanation, and at last gained a co-worker at Troas, saw the vision of Macedonia, and brought the gospel into Europe. The doors You close are to open a greater door.
Lord, we confess that when we are stopped we often doubt You, and when there is no explanation we stop to analyze ourselves. Remove from us the self that insists You follow my plan, and teach us, when stopped, to change the road; at the end of the road, to wait; when we see, to discern together; when it is clear, to set out at once. May the Holy Spirit be our guide for life, and may we obey both in closing and in opening; turn our eyes from our own plans to people’s needs, so that we see those across the sea still waiting for help. May every direction come from You, and all the glory be Yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Setting sail therefore from Troas, we made a straight course to Samothrace, and the day following to Neapolis;
and from there to Philippi, which is a city of Macedonia, the foremost of the district, a Roman colony. We were staying some days in this city.
On the Sabbath day we went outside of the city by a riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down and spoke to the women who had come together.
A certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, one who worshiped God, heard us. The Lord opened her heart to listen to the things which were spoken by Paul.
When she and her household were baptized, she begged us, saying, “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house and stay.” So she persuaded us.
b: In the last devotion, Paul saw the vision of the Macedonian man at Troas, the whole team discerned it together and set out at once, concluding that God had called them to preach the gospel there.

Now the ship set sail. The gospel was to cross the Aegean and, for the first time, set foot on European soil. We would suppose that for so momentous a step God would welcome it with a great revival. But what Luke records is a gathering of a few women by a river, and a woman who sold cloth.
I. “Running a straight course to Samothrace, and the next day to Neapolis”—Two Days of a Favorable Wind
Verse 11: “Setting sail therefore from Troas, we made a straight course to Samothrace, and the next day to Neapolis.”

This sea route was about a hundred and thirty miles, and they covered it in two days. “Made a straight course” in the original means “ran before the wind,” with only one night’s stop on the island of Samothrace. Years later, when Paul went from Philippi back to Troas, the same route took five days (20:6). The same sea, two days going and five days returning—going, the wind was favorable.

In the last devotion the Holy Spirit closed doors twice; in this one He opens doors all the way. When the direction comes from God, even the wind cooperates. This does not mean that a favorable wind is necessarily God’s will, but that one who first obeys when the door is closed will see how God paves the way when it is open.
• A favorable wind confirms: willing to wait earlier, I can recognize the road God opens later.
II. “Philippi… a Roman colony”—A Little Rome
Verse 12: “From there to Philippi, which is a city of Macedonia, the first of the district, a Roman colony.”

Neapolis was the port, and a few miles inland lay Philippi. The city was named for Philip II, father of Alexander the Great; in 42 BC Octavian defeated Caesar’s assassins here and settled his retired veterans in the city afterward, and from then on Philippi was a “Roman colony.” Its residents had Roman citizenship, lived under Roman law, and spoke Latin. It was a little Rome built on Macedonian soil.

In such a city there were very few Jews, so few that there was not even a synagogue—by Jewish rule, ten men were required to form one. Paul’s practice of entering the synagogue first in every city could not work here.

Paul later wrote to the church in this city, “For our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20). The word “citizenship” was exactly the “citizenship” the Philippians were proud of. They were Rome’s colony in Macedonia, and the church was heaven’s colony on earth—this is God’s system: a people who let Jesus be King, in a city where Caesar was king, forming a domain belonging to another kingdom.
• See clearly the city first: in the environment where I am, who is king? To which kingdom does my identity belong?
III. “Outside of the gate by a riverside”—Where Were the Macedonian Men?
Verse 13: “On the Sabbath day we went outside of the city by a riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down and spoke to the women who had come together.”

With no synagogue, they went to the river. Outside the city, by the river, was where a few devout women gathered to pray on the Sabbath. In the vision it was a Macedonian “man” calling, yet on arriving Paul found only a few women. For a person of self, would the gap not seem too great? Several hundred miles walked and a sea crossed, just for these few?

Paul did not think so. He “sat down”—the posture of a Jewish teacher—and, facing a few women, began to preach in earnest. He did not treat them as a stopover, and did not wait for the “real audience” to appear. In his eyes, these few by the river were the Macedonians God had called him to help. People matter more than tasks; however small the scale of the work, the value of the people is not small.
• Don’t despise small scenes: what God gives me is often not the scene I imagined but the few people before me.
• Sit down and preach in earnest: preaching to three and preaching to three thousand call for the same earnestness.
IV. “The Lord opened her heart”—The Woman Who Sold Purple
Verse 14: “A certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, one who worshiped God, heard us, whose heart the Lord opened to listen to the things which were spoken by Paul.”

Lydia was not a local; she came from Thyatira in Asia, a city famous for dyed cloth. Purple cloth was an expensive luxury, its dye extracted from sea snails, a color only princes and nobles could afford. In this trade Lydia was very likely quite wealthy, with her own house and household. “One who worshiped God” means she was a God-fearing Gentile, not yet joined to Judaism but already seeking the true God.

It is interesting: Paul was forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak in Asia, yet the first believer he met in Europe was someone from Asia. God closed that door but brought the person behind the door to Paul.

“The Lord opened her heart.” Luke’s Gospel uses the same word: the risen Lord “opened their minds, that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:45). Paul preached and Lydia listened, but what opened her heart was not Paul’s eloquence but the Lord.

It is like a flower bud. You can water it, loosen the soil, and set it by the window; but you cannot pry the petals open with your hands, which would only ruin it. A flower is opened by sunlight. Lydia’s heart was opened by the Lord, and Paul was only the one standing beside it with water. So “listening” was the result, not the cause—the heart was opened, and only then could a person take it in.
• The Lord is the one who opens hearts: the one who preaches the gospel waters, the one who opens hearts is the Lord, and the credit is His.
• Is my heart open: when I read Scripture and hear sermons today, am I “listening,” or listening with my heart closed?
V. “Come into my house, and stay”—When the Heart Opens, the Door Opens
Verse 15: “When she and her household were baptized, she begged us, saying, ‘If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house, and stay.’ So she persuaded us.”

Lydia believed and her whole household was baptized with her—in that age the household head’s faith decided the direction of the household. And the first thing she did was open her door: she invited Paul’s team to stay at her house. “Persuaded” is a strong word; Luke’s Gospel uses it of the Emmaus disciples who “urged” Jesus to stay (Luke 24:29)—the kind of hospitality that will not take no for an answer.

Her words are interesting too: “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord.” She joined hospitality to faith: if I truly believe, I should open my door; if you judge that I truly believe, come in. The first form of faith is an open door at home.

Her house later became the meeting place of the church in Philippi (16:40). And this church became the only church from which Paul accepted financial support (Philippians 4:15–16). A generous church began with a generous woman.
• When the heart opens, the door opens: since I believed, have my home, my wallet, and my time opened along with it?
• From one person to a church: God used one person willing to open her door to set a whole church in place.
The Light of the 321 Principles: The Lord Opens the Heart, People Open the Door, and the Church Is There

Philippi was a little Rome where Caesar was king. The gospel did not enter by confronting it or by a great revival, but by the Lord opening one woman’s heart and that woman opening the door of her house. God’s system thus made its home in Caesar’s city.

What letting Jesus have all the glory looks like in this passage is clear: Paul preached, yet what Luke records is “the Lord opened her heart.” A preacher who credits people’s believing to his own eloquence, method, and strategy leaves his place and grasps glory that does not belong to him; one who returns to his place knows he is only the one who waters, and the Lord is the one who opens the heart.

And Lydia shows us the first step of self-denial: one whose heart is opened opens what is hers as well. House, business, and family are no longer only “mine.” A person of self, having believed, still keeps the door shut and is spiritual only at church; a person emptied of self, having believed, makes the home a place for the church.
a: Recognize the Favorable Wind
Willing to obey at the closed door earlier, I can recognize the road God opens later.
See the City Clearly
In my environment, who is king? To which kingdom does my identity belong?
Don’t Despise Small Scenes
Speak to the few before me with the same earnestness as to three thousand.
Give the Credit to the Lord Who Opens Hearts
I only water; He is the one who opens hearts.
When the Heart Opens, the Door Opens
Home, wallet, and time open along with faith.
q: “The Lord opened her heart to listen.” The last time you read Scripture or heard a sermon, was your heart open or closed as you listened? Are you willing, today, to ask the Lord first to open your heart and then to open the Bible?

The first thing Lydia did after believing was open her home. Since you believed, which door is still closed—home, wallet, time, or a certain relationship? If the Lord asked you to open it today, what would you do?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that the first step of bringing the gospel into Europe was not a great revival but a prayer gathering of a few women by a river and the opened heart of a woman who sold cloth. Thank You for letting us see that You closed the door of Asia yet brought Lydia of Asia to Philippi; Your plan is far greater than we can see.
Lord, open our hearts too, so that when we read Your word and hear Your teaching today, we listen and do not listen with closed hearts. Remove from us the self that despises small scenes and wants only large audiences; teach us, like Paul, to sit down and preach in earnest to the few before us, and teach us, like Lydia, to open the door the moment the heart opens. May You be King in the city where we live, may we become a domain of Your heavenly kingdom on earth, and may all the glory go to the Lord who opens hearts. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: As we were going to prayer, a certain girl having a spirit of divination met us, who brought her masters much gain by fortune telling.
Following Paul and us, she cried out, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to us a way of salvation!”
She was doing this for many days. But Paul, becoming greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her!” It came out that very hour.
But when her masters saw that the hope of their gain was gone, they seized Paul and Silas, and dragged them into the marketplace before the rulers.
When they had brought them to the magistrates, they said, “These men, being Jews, are agitating our city
and advocate customs which it is not lawful for us to accept or to observe, being Romans.”
The multitude rose up together against them and the magistrates tore their clothes from them, then commanded them to be beaten with rods.
When they had laid many stripes on them, they threw them into prison, charging the jailer to keep them safely,
who, having received such a command, threw them into the inner prison, and secured their feet in the stocks.
b: In the last devotion, the Lord opened Lydia’s heart, and she and her household were baptized and persuaded Paul’s company to stay at her house. The first door in Philippi was open.

But a city where Caesar was king would not stay quiet forever. In this devotion Luke turns the camera from a wealthy woman to a slave girl who had nothing; from a prayer gathering by the river to the marketplace, the court, and the prison. The price of setting her free was the welts on Paul’s and Silas’ backs.
I. “Possessed with a spirit of divination”—A Person Being Used
Verse 16: “As we were going to the place of prayer, a certain girl having a spirit of divination met us, who brought her masters much gain by fortune-telling.”

“Spirit of divination” in the original is “a spirit of Python.” Python was the great serpent of Greek myth that guarded the temple at Delphi, whose spirit was said to possess the priestess there and enable her to prophesy. So in the eyes of the Philippians this girl was one who could contact spirits and tell fortunes. She was a “girl,” a slave; “masters” is plural—she belonged not to one man but to a group of partners.

To these masters she was not a person but a walking cash machine. The torment of being possessed was hers; the money from her predictions was theirs. “Much gain”—Luke uses a heavy word. This was a life oppressed by a demon and squeezed by men, twice bound, with no escape from either.
• See the person, not only the usefulness: around me, is there someone in whom I see only his usefulness and not his pain?
II. “These men are servants of the Most High God”—True Words from the Wrong Mouth
Verses 17 and 18: she followed Paul and his company, crying out, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to you the way of salvation.” For many days.

Strangely, every word she said was true. Paul was indeed a servant of the Most High God, and what he preached was indeed the way of salvation. Why did Paul not accept such “testimony,” and instead become troubled?

Because the source was wrong. “Most High God” in a Gentile’s mouth was a vague title, which could refer to Zeus or to any god; to the Philippians this sounded like one more charlatan advertising for another group of charlatans. The Lord Jesus, when on earth, also would not let demons testify of Him (Mark 1:25), for the same reason: the gospel does not need darkness to endorse it. Truth coming from the wrong mouth actually pulls truth down.

“Troubled” in the original means “deeply grieved”—not merely annoyed at the noise but pained for this person. Paul turned, and what he addressed was not the girl but “the spirit”: “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her!” Not in his own name, not by his own power—the focus was Jesus. The spirit came out “that very hour.”
• Don’t accept praise from the wrong mouth: if pleasant words come from the wrong source, do I want them?
• In the name of Jesus: facing darkness, my weapon is not my experience but His name.
III. “The hope of their gain was gone”—Set Free, They Stepped on the Money
Verse 19: “But when her masters saw that the hope of their gain was gone, they seized Paul and Silas, and dragged them into the marketplace to the rulers.”

A slave girl set free should have been a cause for the whole city to rejoice. Yet one group did not rejoice—her masters. “The hope of their gain” uses the same word as “come out”: the spirit came out, and the hope of money came out with it. Luke’s pen is sharp: to these men, one person’s freedom and their loss were one and the same thing.

Stepping on someone’s money hurts more than stepping on his foot. The silversmiths of Ephesus in chapter 19 were the same, stirring up a riot as soon as they heard their business was affected (19:25–27). Wherever the gospel goes, those who profit from other people’s bondage rise up against it.

Notice that only Paul and Silas were seized. Luke and Timothy were not—very likely because one was a Gentile and the other half Gentile. Persecution never reasons; it seizes only what is easiest to seize.
• Where is my gain: is there any income or advantage of mine built on someone else’s bondage?
• Freeing people has a price: rescuing a person often offends those who profit from him.
IV. “These men, being Jews”—Putting On a Respectable Cloak

Verses 20 to 22: the masters brought Paul before the magistrates, but their charge was not “they drove out our spirit and cost us money.” They said: “These men, being Jews, are agitating our city, and set forth customs which it is not lawful for us to accept or to observe, being Romans.”

Money was never mentioned from beginning to end. They dressed up a dispute over profit as a great matter of race and patriotism. “Jews”—the Emperor Claudius had just expelled the Jews from Rome (18:2), so in a Roman colony the word itself was a crime. “We Romans”—this stirred the whole city’s pride. So “the multitude rose up together against them,” a crowd with nothing to do with it, ignited by two words.

This is exactly the habit of the person of self: the true motive is his own loss, but what is spoken is principle, justice, and the public good. We do this too—what displeases us is that our interests were touched, yet what we say is, “This isn’t proper.” God looks at the heart, not at the cloak.
• Look honestly at my own motive: when I oppose something, is it because it is wrong, or because it touched my interests?
V. “Beaten with rods… into the inner prison, and made their feet secure in the stocks”—The Deepest Cell

Verses 22 to 24: “The magistrates tore their clothes off of them, and commanded them to be beaten with rods. When they had laid many stripes on them, they threw them into prison, charging the jailer to keep them safely, who, having received such a command, threw them into the inner prison, and secured their feet in the stocks.”

The “magistrates” were the two officials of the colony, with attendants who carried bundled rods, the symbol of Roman power. There was no trial and no defense; their clothes were torn off and they were beaten with rods in public. Paul later said he was “beaten with rods three times” (2 Corinthians 11:25), and this was one of them; he also mentioned having been “shamefully treated at Philippi” (1 Thessalonians 2:2). To be stripped and beaten in public, the shame cuts deeper than the pain.

Then came the inner prison—the innermost and darkest cell, their feet in the stocks, wooden shackles that spread the legs apart and held them fast so that one could not even turn over. The passage stops here. Luke does not hurry to the events of midnight; he lets us sit a while in the inner prison first.

For a slave girl’s freedom, two apostles had their backs opened and their feet locked in wood. This is what self-denial looks like most concretely: for Jesus and for others, not for oneself. And the girl? Luke does not mention her again. Paul did not know what became of her, yet he paid the price all the same.
• Pay a price for others: what price have I last paid for someone else’s freedom?
• Sitting in the inner prison: this passage stops at the darkest place, but God’s story has not stopped.
The Light of the 321 Principles: The Focus Is Jesus, and People Matter More Than Profit

There are three kinds of people in this passage. The girl’s masters, who treated a person as a cash machine, whose gain meant her bondage and her freedom meant their loss; the magistrates and the crowd, stirred up by the two words “Jews” and “Romans,” who acted without asking right from wrong; and Paul and Silas, who for a slave girl who would never repay them paid with beating and prison.

People matter more than tasks, and relationships more than things—in the marketplace of Philippi this became a bloody dividing line. A person of self calculates profit, and a person’s worth is decided by usefulness; a person emptied of self sees the person, and even a slave girl possessed by a spirit and squeezed by men is worth paying a price for.

And the sentence by which Paul cast out the spirit is the key to it all: “in the name of Jesus Christ.” He did not free her by his own power, and he did not bear the consequences by his own power. The focus was on Jesus, so he dared to set her free; the focus was on Jesus, so he could sit down in the inner prison. A self-centered person who meets such a price asks, “Is it worth it?” A person who lets Jesus be King asks only, “What does the Lord want me to do?” If the answer is to free that slave girl, the price is left to the Lord.

q: The real reason the girl’s masters opposed the gospel was that “the hope of their gain was gone.” Have you ever opposed something, speaking of principle while the real reason in your heart was your own interest? Are you willing to admit it honestly before the Lord today?
Paul paid with beating and prison for a slave girl who would not repay him. Is there someone for whom the Lord is asking you to pay a little price? Are you willing?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that You saw that slave girl, possessed and squeezed by men, and that Your servants paid with welts and prison for her freedom. Thank You for letting us see that in Your eyes a slave girl’s freedom matters more than a group of men’s profit, and a person matters more than everything.
Lord, search our motives. We often dress our loss as principle and call our interest justice; remove from us the self that treats people as usefulness and loss as right and wrong. Give us Paul’s eyes, to see people’s pain and not only their usefulness; and Paul’s courage, to speak to darkness in Your name and to pay a price for others’ freedom. When our obedience takes us into the inner prison, make us remember that Your story has not stopped. May every release come in Your name, and all the glory be Yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
